excerpts.text: Brachial plexus injury: Perioperative brachial plexus injury is most often linked to positioning that increases plexus tension, classically, marked shoulder abduction (often beyond 90°), combined with external rotation, posterior displacement of the shoulder, or contralateral neck rotation/extension. Prone cases, wide arm placement on arm boards, and insufficient padding can further lower the threshold for injury. The clinical picture can range from predominantly sensory complaints to substantial weakness, depending on which trunks or cords are affected. Patients may report shoulder or supraclavicular discomfort, paresthesias radiating down the arm, and difficulty with tasks requiring shoulder abduction, elbow flexion/extension, or fine hand function. On examination, weakness that spans more than one named peripheral nerve distribution should prompt consideration of a plexopathy rather than an isolated mononeuropathy.

excerpts.text: Adson test: The arm to be examined of the seated or standing patient is abducted 30° at the shoulder and maximally extended. The radial pulse is monitored by the examiner, who grasps the patient’s wrist. The patient is then asked to extend the neck and turn the head toward the symptomatic side, taking a deep breath and holding it. The examiner then compares the radial pulse in this position. The test is defined as positive when a marked decrease or disappearance of the radial pulse is observed. A comparative test on the non-affected side is recommended.

excerpts.text: Imaging of the thoracic outlet often requires specific protocols and positioning that is not inherent in standard CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) neck, cervical spine, or chest protocols. CT evaluation of TOS is typically performed in “neutral” and “stressed” positions. Images are obtained from the elbow to the aortic arch with the arms adducted (neutral), followed by abduction (stressed) and repeat imaging. When contrast is indicated, scan acquisition is typically performed with a contralateral antecubital intravenous (IV) injection, with either an empiric scan delay of 15 to 20 s or bolus tracking over the ascending aorta. Some centers add the additional step of placing the contralateral arm in abduction (with the symptomatic ipsilateral arm in the neutral position) in order to minimize streak artifact.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 31-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of tingling sensations in his right medial forearm and three ulnar digits. These sensations intensified when lying on his right side and when raising his right arm overhead, such as during hair washing. Neurological examination revealed normal muscle strength and sensory function in his right upper extremities, with no muscle atrophy observed in the intrinsic muscles of his right hand. Tinel's test was negative for the right supraclavicular fossa. During a posture involving 90° abduction and external rotation of the shoulder, pain in his right palm and forearm increased, and his right palm became pale. An electrophysiological study from a local community hospital was reviewed, showing no abnormalities in nerve conduction studies, including the MABC nerve, when using the reference values of our institute. Needle EMG results were also normal. Cervical spine plain radiograph revealed an anomalous right first rib, which was upwardly convex with its anterior tip fused to the second rib.. Confirmed diagnosis: Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome and Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome and Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

excerpts.text: One of the important first steps in radiographically evaluating the painful hip is to assess for the presence of degenerative changes. This affects treatment decisions, given the limited role for hip preservation in advanced osteoarthritis. The Tönnis classification is commonly used to grade progressive degrees of degenerative changes as visualized on the AP pelvis radiograph. Grade 0 involves no signs of osteoarthritis. Grade 1 includes slight joint space narrowing, lipping at the joint margin, and increased sclerosis at the femoral head and acetabulum. Grade 2 includes increased joint space narrowing, small cysts in the femoral head or acetabulum, and moderate loss of femoral head sphericity. Grade 3 includes severe joint space narrowing or joint space obliteration, large cysts in the femoral head or acetabulum, severe femoral head deformity, and evidence of avascular necrosis. Although there is a lack of consensus on its reliability (particularly at early stages of arthritis when distinguishing between grades 0 and 1), it nevertheless provides an efficient way to assess for the presence of degenerative changes and to rule out severe osteoarthritis.

This value is calculated as the percentage of the total femoral head width that lies lateral to the lateralmost portion of the acetabulum (rather than the lateral edge of the acetabular sourcil which may lay further medial). A normal hip is defined as having an extrusion index of <25%, and higher values are thought to be associated with acetabular dysplasia. This measure is closely geometrically related to the LCEA value and correlates highly.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 4-month-old girl presented with right-sided neck muscle tightness and a right brachial plexus injury. An ultrasonogram from a previous hospital showed diffuse thickening and heterogeneous hyperechogenicity in the right sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM) compared to the left. She was born at full term via vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3,640 grams, and her birth was complicated by cephalhematoma and a right brachial plexus injury. Initial clinical examination revealed a tight and thick right SCM. Despite receiving physical therapy for 3 months at the previous hospital, there was no improvement in her neck motion range. Neck rotation was measured using an arthrodial protractor with the patient lying supine, shoulders stabilized, and head and neck supported in a neutral position. Lateral flexion was measured with a large protractor, showing 50° of neck rotation to the right and 40° of lateral flexion to the left, resulting in right torticollis. The patient also exhibited weakness in the right shoulder girdle muscles and elbow flexors, scoring grade 2 on pediatric functional muscle testing. Induced developmental reflexes showed partial movement, also graded as 2. Additionally,. Confirmed diagnosis: Low-Grade Fibromyxoid Sarcoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Low-Grade Fibromyxoid Sarcoma.

excerpts.text: Although obtaining negative surgical margins is the primary goal of head and neck surgery, achieving this may be impossible in some cases because of infiltration of vital structures such as the carotid artery or the prevertebral fasciae. The positive surgical margin status is associated with decreased survival, therefore a patient should be re-operated if the tumor was not removed completely. However, achieving negative margins can cause impairment in important functions such as chewing, swallowing and speech, and adversely affect quality of life. Therefore primary radiochemotherapy is an alternative for patients with advanced head and neck carcinomas.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 43-year-old Caucasian male experienced 5 months of ongoing posterior cervical neck pain extending to the right shoulder, along with paresthesias and right upper extremity radiculopathy. Despite normal motor and sensory exams, he exhibited diffuse hyperreflexia (3+ bilateral biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patella, and ankles with two beats of unsustained clonus in his right foot) and bilateral Babinski signs. Hoffman’s signs were negative on both sides. Cervical MRI revealed a T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, enhancing intradural, extramedullary mass measuring 2.4 × 1.4 × 1.1 cm at the C5–C6 level. The mass was eccentrically positioned to the right, compressing the cervical spinal cord without abnormal hyperintense T2 spinal cord signal. The patient underwent a cervical laminectomy for gross total microsurgical resection of the tumor. The tumor was intradural, completely extramedullary, and appeared to originate from a C6 nerve rootlet. Gross total resection of the tumor was achieved and the entire lesion was sent for further analysis.. Confirmed diagnosis: pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. Differential diagnosis includes: pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.

Nocturnal leg cramps are relieved with stretching or walking, but no urge to move is experienced, and painful muscular contraction is clearly unlike RLS sensations. Positional discomfort comes on with prolonged sitting or lying in the same position, but it is usually relieved by a simple change in position, unlike RLS, without a true circadian pattern, if not because during the night the rest increases the chances to maintain the same position. excerpts.text: Presentation: A 96-year-old female with a history of hypertension and severe dementia experienced a subacute onset of swelling and pain in her right arm after waking up. Due to her advanced dementia, obtaining a comprehensive history and conducting a thorough physical examination was challenging. However, it was confirmed by her caregiver that her right arm appeared normal the previous night, and she had slept with her right arm under her head. On examination, her right arm exhibited severe purpura and skin tension, but the radial artery was palpable. An orthopedist referred her to the cardiovascular department. Computed tomography did not show any significant stenosis of the right subclavian vein. Ultrasonography performed in both normal and abduction positions also did not reveal any significant findings. Additionally, neither computed tomography nor ultrasonography detected any thrombus in the proximal or distal right subclavian vein. Despite these findings, her unilateral edema resembled that of a venous disorder, prompting further imaging of the right brachial vein in both normal and abduction positions. Significant stenosis was seen in the latter position.. Confirmed diagnosis: Venous Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Venous Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 37-year-old male experienced recurring pressure-like discomfort in the left side of the chest, extending to the neck and shoulder, along with numbness and tingling in the left arm. These symptoms were sometimes worsened by shoulder movements. During the physical examination, tenderness was noted along the medial scapula, and there was a reduction in the abduction of the left shoulder. Minimal pain was observed during impingement tests, including Neer and Hawkins exams. The Adson’s test was positive, while the cross-body and O’Brien’s exams were negative. Cardiac evaluations, including electrocardiogram and stress echocardiogram, showed no abnormalities. Both regular computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging results were unremarkable. The patient's symptoms did not improve with physical therapy. A vascular duplex of left upper extremity showed compression of both the subclavian vein and artery. The subclavian vein was assessed with color and spectral Doppler in the neutral position, at 90° and 180° abduction. At both 90° and 180° abduction, there was loss of cardiac pulsatility and respiratory phasicity, but continuous flow remained, indicating compression without obstruc. Confirmed diagnosis: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

excerpts.text: Adson test: The arm to be examined of the seated or standing patient is abducted 30° at the shoulder and maximally extended. The radial pulse is monitored by the examiner, who grasps the patient’s wrist. The patient is then asked to extend the neck and turn the head toward the symptomatic side, taking a deep breath and holding it. The examiner then compares the radial pulse in this position. The test is defined as positive when a marked decrease or disappearance of the radial pulse is observed. A comparative test on the non-affected side is recommended.

excerpts.text: Imaging of the thoracic outlet often requires specific protocols and positioning that is not inherent in standard CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) neck, cervical spine, or chest protocols. CT evaluation of TOS is typically performed in “neutral” and “stressed” positions. Images are obtained from the elbow to the aortic arch with the arms adducted (neutral), followed by abduction (stressed) and repeat imaging. When contrast is indicated, scan acquisition is typically performed with a contralateral antecubital intravenous (IV) injection, with either an empiric scan delay of 15 to 20 s or bolus tracking over the ascending aorta. Some centers add the additional step of placing the contralateral arm in abduction (with the symptomatic ipsilateral arm in the neutral position) in order to minimize streak artifact.

excerpts.text: Lung CT scan has been used to understand the pathophysiology and the interplay with mechanical ventilation. CT scan clearly showed that ARDS is a non-homogeneous lung disease with the following classically reported morphological patterns: consolidated regions (defined by a homogenous increase in density without vessels or bronchi), ground glass areas (with an increase in density with still recognizable vessels) and the normal aerated regions. These three morphological features are usually simultaneously present. Air bronchograms and small pleural effusions are also common. The dependent localization of consolidated areas is related to the increase in lung oedema (i.e. increase in lung weight) during the initial phase of ARDS which raises the hydrostatic pressure transmitted throughout the lung, causing a reduction in lung gas volume and the development of non-aerated lung regions. These poorly or non-aerated lung regions are characterized by a higher inflammation than normally ventilated lung regions. The presence of non-inflated areas causes a major expansion of the neighbouring lung regions and generation of higher local pressures which act as a “stress raiser”. Higher amounts of inhomogeneities are accompanied by higher stress raisers and severity of ARDS and worse outcome. Pulmonary ARDS presents a similar amount of consolidated and ground glass areas while extrapulmonary ARDS has a higher amount of ground glass areas. Presentation: A 47-year-old female presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. An MRI of the lumbar spine performed at an outside institution revealed a mass-like lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen. The patient was managed with analgesics over a 1-month period, resulting in partial symptom resolution. She later visited the emergency department due to persistent symptoms, where another MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted sequences) was obtained. No contrast injection was performed as it is not part of the low back pain/radiculopathy investigation protocol in the emergency department. It showed the previously described lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen, as well as other ipsilateral lesions in the posterior paraspinal muscles and the anterior epidural space. Most of the lesions had a mass-like appearance and low signal intensity in all MR sequences. One lesion in the posterior paravertebral muscle showed mixed signal intensity on T2 weighted sequence, defining a fluid–fluid level. All the lesions were unchanged compared with the outside scan. The CT scan confirmed the calcified nature of the lesions and also showed no contrast enhancement. It also contributed to an addit. Confirmed diagnosis: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Differential diagnosis includes: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Preeclampsia (PE) is defined as gestational hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90 mm Hg) accompanied by ≥1 of the following new-onset conditions at ≥20 weeks of gestation: proteinuria, acute kidney injury (a serum creatinine level ≥ 90 μmol/L), increased hepatic transaminases, a platelet count < 100 g/L, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemolysis, fetal growth restriction, an abnormal umbilical artery Doppler wave form analysis, or stillbirth. Eclampsia, in addition to the criteria defining preeclampsia, is characterized by altered mental status, blindness, stroke, clonus, severe headache, and persistent visual scotomata. Although HELLP syndrome arises in women with hypertension and proteinuria, in 10–20% of cases, these signs are absent. However, it must be considered part of the pathophysiologic spectrum of preeclampsia; therefore, where the signs and symptoms of the syndrome arise, the signs and symptoms of preeclampsia should also be sought. Excessive weight gain and generalized edema precede approximately 50% of the manifestations of the syndrome. As with preeclampsia, the pathogenetic origin lies in abnormal placentation, but compared with preeclampsia there is an excessive hepatic inflammatory response and excessive coagulatory activation. Elevated circulating levels of the trophoblast-originated anti-angiogenic mediators, soluble endoglin, and the soluble form of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (sFlt1), which are the mediators of endothelial dysfunction, have been detected in PE/HELLP syndrome.

Presentation: A 73-year-old man presented with a sore throat, hoarseness, and weight loss. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 30-mm type 0-IIc lesion on the posterior wall of the cardia of the stomach with an estimated depth reaching the muscularis propria (T2). An upper gastrointestinal series showed deformation of the posterior wall of the cardia, indicating involvement of the muscularis propria (T2). Biopsy showed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cells. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) identified an enlarged lymph node in the left subclavian region, and a positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) scan showed mild FDG accumulation in the same lymph node (SUV-max 3.7). No other obvious lymph node or distant metastasis findings were observed. The cervical lymph nodes were not palpable, and blood tests showed normal levels of tumor markers and other variables. A left subclavian lymph node biopsy was performed to determine the treatment strategy. Due to the proximity of cervical blood vessels and the risk of recurrent nerve injury, the biopsy was conducted under general anesthesia. The tumor was an elastic, firm, well-defined mass, approximately 20 mm in ma. Confirmed diagnosis: Schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Schwannoma.

The main symptom described in classic AINS is the partial or full disappearance of pinch grip between the thumb and index finger, usually unilaterally. Loss of PQ strength is more difficult to notice. AIN is a motor nerve, so no sensory alterations occur. Prodromal pain in the shoulder, arm, or elbow may be present. The aetiologies of anatomical compression, physical exertion, repetitive activity, infection, vaccination, pregnancy, supracondylar humerus fracture on children, sleeping on an arm, forearm immobilization, and surgery unrelated to AIN (e.g., shoulder arthroscopy) have been described, but sometimes there is no apparent cause.

There is limited evidence and no strong recommendation for the use of antiplatelet agents or long-term anticoagulation therapy in RP management. However, short-term low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) anticoagulation may be used in specific cases of acute limb ischemia. A single placebo-controlled study by Denton et al. involving 30 patients showed that LMWH reduced the severity of RP symptoms, but this finding has not been replicated in other studies.

Upon admission, she was found to be somnolent and moderately dehydrated, exhibiting right-sided hemiparesis and hemihypoesthesia. Presentation: A 66-year-old man presented with a 15-year history of neck, supraclavicular, and right shoulder pain, along with numbness and weakness in the right arm. He underwent C3–6 posterior decompression with laminoplasty and internal fixation, followed by lumbar dynamic transpedicle fixation for lumbar disc herniation 6 months later. Post-surgery, he was unable to walk without assistance, and there was minimal improvement in arm weakness and numbness. Physical examination showed muscle weakness (Lovett grade 2/5) in the intrinsic muscles of the right hand, decreased grasp strength, and significantly reduced sensation in the ulnar part of the forearm. A positive Adson test result and minor muscle atrophy of the thenar muscles were observed. Arm abduction was limited to 30°, preventing full conduction of the Wright and Roos tests. In the Adson test posture, slight C-8 radiculopathy was noted. Electrodiagnostic studies demonstrated lower trunk axonal loss.. Confirmed diagnosis: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

The consensus process arrived at a two‐step GLIM procedure that starts with nutrition screening followed by diagnostic assessment for confirmation of malnutrition. In patients identified as being at risk of malnutrition, all five GLIM criteria should be assessed to confirm the presence of malnutrition. Three phenotypic and two etiologic criteria were selected from existing widely accepted approaches to diagnosis. All chosen criteria are well‐established nutrition‐related variables that, in their own capacity, have well‐validated prognostic value for negative clinical outcomes—ie, mortality. The three phenotypic criteria are nonvolitional weight loss, low body mass index (BMI), and low muscle mass, whereas the two etiologic criteria are reduced food intake/food assimilation and disease burden/inflammation. To confirm a malnutrition diagnosis, at least one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion must be present. Still, in occasional cases, it will not be possible to assess all five criteria. When assessment of one or more criteria is not possible for compelling practical reasons, the diagnosis of malnutrition will still be possible if, among those available, one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion are fulfilled. For exclusion of the diagnosis, all five criteria need to be assessed. Further, the severity grading of malnutrition is based solely on the phenotypic criteria. When the criteria assessment confirms the diagnosis of malnutrition, the patient should undergo a comprehensive nutrition assessment, according to available resources, to establish a treatment plan. Presentation: A 60-year-old female with a three-year history of abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss presented for evaluation of worsening symptoms. Presentation: A 34-year-old male with no known co-morbidities presented to the hospital with complaints of weakness in the left arm and pain in the left upper limb for one month. excerpts.text: Presentation: A 66-year-old Japanese male reported weakness in his left fingers and hand, without any issues in walking or symptoms in the lower extremities one year ago. Compressive lesions in the cervical spine were identified at the C5-C7 level. The manual muscle test (MMT) of his left hand was grade 2, and he opted for conservative therapy as his right hand was dominant. One year later, he experienced weakness in his right fingers and hand (MMT grade 2) without pain or numbness. Pulses of the radial artery were confirmed at the initial presentation. Magnetic resonance imaging indicated a more severe compressive lesion at the C5-C6 level compared to one year ago. Computed tomography (CT) showed a difference in the attachment to the Th1 vertebrae between the right and left first ribs, and the presence of a joint between the first rib and the second rib. Two weeks after the onset of right-hand weakness, he developed a sloping shoulder, a weak pulse of the radial artery, pain, and gangrene in his right hand. Laboratory data showed inflammation with a white blood cell count of 17,500/μl and C-reactive protein level of 19.34 mg/dl. D-dimer levels were 1.1 ng/ml.. Confirmed diagnosis: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome with Subclavian Arterial Thrombosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome with Subclavian Arterial Thrombosis.

excerpts.text: Brachial plexus injury: Perioperative brachial plexus injury is most often linked to positioning that increases plexus tension, classically, marked shoulder abduction (often beyond 90°), combined with external rotation, posterior displacement of the shoulder, or contralateral neck rotation/extension. Prone cases, wide arm placement on arm boards, and insufficient padding can further lower the threshold for injury. The clinical picture can range from predominantly sensory complaints to substantial weakness, depending on which trunks or cords are affected. Patients may report shoulder or supraclavicular discomfort, paresthesias radiating down the arm, and difficulty with tasks requiring shoulder abduction, elbow flexion/extension, or fine hand function. On examination, weakness that spans more than one named peripheral nerve distribution should prompt consideration of a plexopathy rather than an isolated mononeuropathy.

excerpts.text: Chronicity is a hallmark of DM. It is conceivable that the decrease in SROM observed in many DM patients are parallel processes of aging and an accelerated muscle skeletal degeneration. Support for this hypothesis comes from a study suggesting DM has an additive negative effect on limited joint mobility, but no significant correlation with the duration of DM. In addition, Cole et al. found no significant difference in prevalence of shoulder pain/stiffness between DM and non-DM subjects after adjustment for age, sex, smoking and obesity.

On plain radiographs, it is essential to examine for bony avulsion or calcification of the medial collateral ligament, osteophyte of the olecranon, arthritic changes, and loose bodies. Calcification and olecranon osteophytes are the most frequently observed findings, appearing in more than 50% of cases. A discrepancy of more than 0.5 mm compared to the unaffected side on the valgus stress view may suggest a complete or severe partial tear of the medial collateral ligament. However, it has been noted that the medial joint gap is approximately 0.32 mm wider than the valgus stress test in the dominant arm of pitchers. Therefore, caution is required, as many athletes exhibit valgus laxity without any specific symptoms. Currently, MRI is acknowledged as an exceptional diagnostic tool for medial collateral ligament injuries, with its sensitivity increasing to 92% and specificity to 100% when combined with an intraarticular arthrogram. Although it is possible to identify medial collateral ligament injuries through ultrasonography, the interpretation may vary depending on the expertise of the examiner.

Presentation: A 43-year-old Caucasian male experienced 5 months of ongoing posterior cervical neck pain extending to the right shoulder, along with paresthesias and right upper extremity radiculopathy. Despite normal motor and sensory exams, he exhibited diffuse hyperreflexia (3+ bilateral biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patella, and ankles with two beats of unsustained clonus in his right foot) and bilateral Babinski signs. Hoffman’s signs were negative on both sides. Cervical MRI revealed a T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense, enhancing intradural, extramedullary mass measuring 2.4 × 1.4 × 1.1 cm at the C5–C6 level. The mass was eccentrically positioned to the right, compressing the cervical spinal cord without abnormal hyperintense T2 spinal cord signal. The patient underwent a cervical laminectomy for gross total microsurgical resection of the tumor. The tumor was intradural, completely extramedullary, and appeared to originate from a C6 nerve rootlet. Gross total resection of the tumor was achieved and the entire lesion was sent for further analysis.. Confirmed diagnosis: pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. Differential diagnosis includes: pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.

Presentation: Case 1: a 46-year-old female experiencing persistent pain in the cervical spine, head, and left upper arm for two years, with increasing severity. She required significant pain medication. Clinical examination indicated a limited range of motion in the cervical spine and sensory radicular symptoms corresponding to the C4-C6 nerve roots. Laboratory tests did not indicate the presence of a tumor or infection.. Confirmed diagnosis: Aggressive Osteoblastoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Aggressive Osteoblastoma.

Headaches, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, and nausea/vomiting are better predictors of life-threatening complications than worsening laboratory parameters. The spontaneous rupture of a subcapsular spathecular hematoma is rare in pregnancy but can be maternally life-threatening in 1 in 40,000/250,000 pregnancies, and approximately 1–2% of these cases occur in the presence of HELLP syndrome. Rupture most often occurs in the right hepatic lobe, and the symptoms are pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen radiating to the back, pain in the right shoulder, anemia, and hypotension. This event can be diagnosed via ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI. Perinatal mortality and morbidity are considerably high and mainly depend on the time of gestation of the event. The perinatal mortality rate is estimated to be between 7.4% and 34%. The main causes of mortality are prematurity, placental insufficiency with or without fetal growth retardation, and placental abruption. With liver rupture, mortality can reach 80%. Neonatal thrombocytopenia occurs in 15–38% of cases and is an important risk factor for neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage as well as long-term neurologic outcomes.

Both neurogenic and vascular components may contribute to TOS symptoms: compression of the subclavian vein and artery causes edema, swelling, cyanosis, and decreased blood flow to the arms; on the other hand, pain, dysesthesia, numbness, and weakness are usually due to neurogenic involvement.

Presentation: A 24-year-old Caucasian female arrived at the emergency department with right arm pain persisting for four days. The pain originated in her neck, extending to the right trapezius and down to her elbow. She had previously visited another emergency department two days earlier and received dexamethasone, cyclobenzaprine, and ibuprofen for a pinched nerve. Despite this treatment, her pain intensified, and she observed positional color changes in her arm, with her hand turning blue unless elevated above her head. Her medical history included menstrual migraines and long-term use of oral contraception since adolescence. She reported no use of tobacco or recreational drugs and consumed alcohol socially. She maintained a regular exercise routine, though the specific type was not detailed. Her family medical history included cervical cancer in her mother, polycythemia in her grandfather, and diabetes, hypertension, and biliary duct cancer in her grandmother. She had allergies to penicillin, latex, and adhesive tape. Laboratory tests showed normal results except for a leukocytosis of 14.4 k/mm3 and neutrophils of 12.1 k/mm3. A chest X-ray revealed no acute cardiopulmonary abnormalities.. Confirmed diagnosis: Venous Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Venous Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

Presentation: A 37-year-old male experienced recurring pressure-like discomfort in the left side of the chest, extending to the neck and shoulder, along with numbness and tingling in the left arm. These symptoms were sometimes worsened by shoulder movements. During the physical examination, tenderness was noted along the medial scapula, and there was a reduction in the abduction of the left shoulder. Minimal pain was observed during impingement tests, including Neer and Hawkins exams. The Adson’s test was positive, while the cross-body and O’Brien’s exams were negative. Cardiac evaluations, including electrocardiogram and stress echocardiogram, showed no abnormalities. Both regular computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging results were unremarkable. The patient's symptoms did not improve with physical therapy. A vascular duplex of left upper extremity showed compression of both the subclavian vein and artery. The subclavian vein was assessed with color and spectral Doppler in the neutral position, at 90° and 180° abduction. At both 90° and 180° abduction, there was loss of cardiac pulsatility and respiratory phasicity, but continuous flow remained, indicating compression without obstruc. Confirmed diagnosis: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

Ulnar-sided numbness in the hand can be a result of compression anywhere from the C8 level, through the thoracic outlet to the hand. In addition to the clinical triad, a careful assessment of the distribution of numbness – ulnar hand, ulnar forearm, ulnar upper arm, shoulder – is essential to stage the level of nerve affliction in these patients.

Presentation: A 15-year-old male reported experiencing weakness, pain, and difficulty in lifting objects with the left arm over the past two weeks. There was no reported history of fever, trauma, or repetitive use of the left arm. Physical examination revealed that all pulses in the left arm were very weak, while pulses in other areas were normal. The systemic examination did not show any abnormalities. A chest X-ray was noted to be unremarkable.. Confirmed diagnosis: Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

Brachial plexus injury: Perioperative brachial plexus injury is most often linked to positioning that increases plexus tension, classically, marked shoulder abduction (often beyond 90°), combined with external rotation, posterior displacement of the shoulder, or contralateral neck rotation/extension. Prone cases, wide arm placement on arm boards, and insufficient padding can further lower the threshold for injury. The clinical picture can range from predominantly sensory complaints to substantial weakness, depending on which trunks or cords are affected. Patients may report shoulder or supraclavicular discomfort, paresthesias radiating down the arm, and difficulty with tasks requiring shoulder abduction, elbow flexion/extension, or fine hand function. On examination, weakness that spans more than one named peripheral nerve distribution should prompt consideration of a plexopathy rather than an isolated mononeuropathy.

Presentation: A 22-year-old man experienced severe left shoulder pain upon waking, which later extended to severe arm pain. Initially, he was diagnosed with a shoulder sprain and placed in a sling, despite no evidence of trauma. The pain persisted, leading to the prescription of multiple medications including paracetamol, gabapentin 600 mg three times daily, and hydrocodone 5 mg three times daily as needed. Two weeks later, he developed hand and arm weakness and was evaluated. Examination revealed 2/5 wrist extension, 3/5 finger flexion, 2/5 abduction of the fifth digit, and 4/5 shoulder abduction, with no scapular winging. Pin prick testing showed no sensory loss along the dermatomes. An electrodiagnostic study conducted a month after onset indicated denervation in multiple muscles innervated by the median, ulnar, radial, and axillary nerves. MRI of the brachial plexus with and without contrast revealed patchy T2 hyperintense signals involving all trunks of the left brachial plexus, with no enhancement observed with contrast. The patient was managed conservatively with physical therapy and gabapentin 300 mg three times daily for neuropathic pain. Two months later, he reported dry eyes and dry m. Confirmed diagnosis: Sjögren syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Sjögren syndrome.

The most common referral indication for brachial plexus ultrasound seems to be to exclude brachial plexus pathology in patients with non-specific arm pain and weakness. For these patients and other patients with normal brachial plexus examinations, a brief report such as “Unremarkable appearances of brachial plexus from the roots to the axilla” is given. For brachial plexopathy, grade the severity of perineural fibrosis as mild, moderate, or severe and state which parts of the brachial plexus are most affected. For suspected malignancy, give an indication as to how confident you are regarding the presence of metastatic infiltration and suggest biopsy, follow-up, or further work-up if unsure.

A fracture of the clavicle during birth may induce a positional preference in the first weeks of life and, as such, may cause an asymmetry. A perinatal fracture can be an option in the differential diagnostics of asymmetry during the first weeks of life. A co-incidence with other perinatal injuries (like brachial plexus injury) was described by Perlow et al.. The obstetric brachial plexus lesion is described separately. The incidence varies between 0.1 and 3.5%, and these fractures usually consolidate within 3 weeks without complications. The clinical presentation can be asymptomatic. When symptomatic, signs include: decreased or absent movement and pain, or tenderness on movement of the arm on the affected side and palpable irregularity along the clavicle.

Presentation: A 44-year-old male experienced a four-day history of progressively worsening left-sided chest wall pain extending to the left shoulder and arm, also affecting the upper back on the same side. The pain began without any apparent cause, worsened at night, and did not improve with over-the-counter painkillers. The pain became severe enough to necessitate emergency services. Paramedics administered glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray, which temporarily alleviated the pain. The chest pain was described as a crushing sensation, while the arm pain was described as pulsating and shooting. The pain intensified around the left scapula, radiating down the ulnar side of the forearm to the medial one and a half digits, eventually spreading over the dorsum of the forearm and the rest of the digits, followed by paraesthesia. Any movement of the upper limb caused severe pain. Blood tests, including full blood count, C-reactive protein (CRP), inflammatory markers, renal function, liver function tests, and troponin cardiac enzyme, were all within normal limits. Due to the chest pain migrating to the left side, the patient was admitted to rule out cardiac causes. An electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogra. Confirmed diagnosis: Brachial Neuritis. Differential diagnosis includes: Brachial Neuritis.

Presentation: A 34-year-old male with no known co-morbidities presented to the hospital with complaints of weakness in the left arm and pain in the left upper limb for one month. There was a history of COVID-19 vaccination (Covishield) immediately prior to the onset of symptoms. On examination, there was a loss of shoulder contour. There was weakness of rotator cuff muscles, especially the supraspinatus muscle, confirmed with positive empty can test and drop arm test. The patient was unable to abduct his arm even against gravity. The neurological examination of distal muscles to the elbow of the left upper limb was normal. The patient was further evaluated with x-rays of the cervical spine and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine.. Confirmed diagnosis: Post-vaccination brachial plexus neuropraxia. Differential diagnosis includes: Post-vaccination brachial plexus neuropraxia.

The main symptoms are pain and limited range of motion in the elbow joint, which gradually intensify as arthritis advances. Until the disease reaches its end-stage, pain typically manifests at the point of maximum extension (posterior pain) or flexion (anterior pain), and is often absent in the mid-range of motion. Pain during extension is a symptom triggered by the mechanical impingement of the olecranon apex and the olecranon fossa. In severe instances, this may hinder the ability to extend the arm in daily activities. Accompanied by ulnar neuropathy, progression of the condition may result in numbness of the fourth and fifth fingers, or even atrophy of the intrinsic finger muscles.

Lung CT scan has been used to understand the pathophysiology and the interplay with mechanical ventilation. CT scan clearly showed that ARDS is a non-homogeneous lung disease with the following classically reported morphological patterns: consolidated regions (defined by a homogenous increase in density without vessels or bronchi), ground glass areas (with an increase in density with still recognizable vessels) and the normal aerated regions. These three morphological features are usually simultaneously present. Air bronchograms and small pleural effusions are also common. The dependent localization of consolidated areas is related to the increase in lung oedema (i.e. increase in lung weight) during the initial phase of ARDS which raises the hydrostatic pressure transmitted throughout the lung, causing a reduction in lung gas volume and the development of non-aerated lung regions. These poorly or non-aerated lung regions are characterized by a higher inflammation than normally ventilated lung regions. The presence of non-inflated areas causes a major expansion of the neighbouring lung regions and generation of higher local pressures which act as a “stress raiser”. Higher amounts of inhomogeneities are accompanied by higher stress raisers and severity of ARDS and worse outcome. Pulmonary ARDS presents a similar amount of consolidated and ground glass areas while extrapulmonary ARDS has a higher amount of ground glass areas. Presentation: A 47-year-old female presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. An MRI of the lumbar spine performed at an outside institution revealed a mass-like lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen. The patient was managed with analgesics over a 1-month period, resulting in partial symptom resolution. She later visited the emergency department due to persistent symptoms, where another MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted sequences) was obtained. No contrast injection was performed as it is not part of the low back pain/radiculopathy investigation protocol in the emergency department. It showed the previously described lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen, as well as other ipsilateral lesions in the posterior paraspinal muscles and the anterior epidural space. Most of the lesions had a mass-like appearance and low signal intensity in all MR sequences. One lesion in the posterior paravertebral muscle showed mixed signal intensity on T2 weighted sequence, defining a fluid–fluid level. All the lesions were unchanged compared with the outside scan. The CT scan confirmed the calcified nature of the lesions and also showed no contrast enhancement. It also contributed to an addit. Confirmed diagnosis: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Differential diagnosis includes: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Preeclampsia (PE) is defined as gestational hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90 mm Hg) accompanied by ≥1 of the following new-onset conditions at ≥20 weeks of gestation: proteinuria, acute kidney injury (a serum creatinine level ≥ 90 μmol/L), increased hepatic transaminases, a platelet count < 100 g/L, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemolysis, fetal growth restriction, an abnormal umbilical artery Doppler wave form analysis, or stillbirth. Eclampsia, in addition to the criteria defining preeclampsia, is characterized by altered mental status, blindness, stroke, clonus, severe headache, and persistent visual scotomata. Although HELLP syndrome arises in women with hypertension and proteinuria, in 10–20% of cases, these signs are absent. However, it must be considered part of the pathophysiologic spectrum of preeclampsia; therefore, where the signs and symptoms of the syndrome arise, the signs and symptoms of preeclampsia should also be sought. Excessive weight gain and generalized edema precede approximately 50% of the manifestations of the syndrome. As with preeclampsia, the pathogenetic origin lies in abnormal placentation, but compared with preeclampsia there is an excessive hepatic inflammatory response and excessive coagulatory activation. Elevated circulating levels of the trophoblast-originated anti-angiogenic mediators, soluble endoglin, and the soluble form of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (sFlt1), which are the mediators of endothelial dysfunction, have been detected in PE/HELLP syndrome.

Case 1 The first pregnancy, followed-up in another hospital, was conceived spontaneously and was reported to be uneventful for the first 5 months until the diagnosis of fetal growth restriction (FGR) due to fetal biometry below the 3rd centile, and ventriculomegaly confirmed by fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A cesarean section was performed at 31 weeks’ gestation due to severe FGR. At birth, a female baby weighted 930 g (< 3rd centile), was 33 cm (<< 3rd centile) in length and with a head circumference of 27.5 cm (3rd–10th centile). The APGAR score was 7/8/8 at the 1′, 5′ and 10′ min of life, respectively. The physical examination showed some peculiar facial dysmorphisms, including microphthalmia, high nasal root and micrognathia. She presented with congenital generalized arthrogryposis with multiples contractures and hypertonia. The baby needed oxygen supplementation for respiratory distress and was then admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. The neonatal MRI confirmed the ventriculomegaly and detected a hypoplastic cerebellar vermis. In addition, there was a cataract in the right eye, while fundus oculi were bilaterally normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed hyperechogenic kidneys. The electrocardiogram and the echocardiogram were normal with a physiologically patent foramen ovale. She presented with feeding difficulties, requiring positioning of a feeding-tube. Severe failure to thrive was due to worsening of general condition. She died because of superimposed kidney failure and pulmonary haemorrhage at 2 months of life. The family refused autopsy. Postnatal

Presentation: A 73-year-old man presented with a sore throat, hoarseness, and weight loss. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 30-mm type 0-IIc lesion on the posterior wall of the cardia of the stomach with an estimated depth reaching the muscularis propria (T2). An upper gastrointestinal series showed deformation of the posterior wall of the cardia, indicating involvement of the muscularis propria (T2). Biopsy showed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cells. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) identified an enlarged lymph node in the left subclavian region, and a positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) scan showed mild FDG accumulation in the same lymph node (SUV-max 3.7). No other obvious lymph node or distant metastasis findings were observed. The cervical lymph nodes were not palpable, and blood tests showed normal levels of tumor markers and other variables. A left subclavian lymph node biopsy was performed to determine the treatment strategy. Due to the proximity of cervical blood vessels and the risk of recurrent nerve injury, the biopsy was conducted under general anesthesia. The tumor was an elastic, firm, well-defined mass, approximately 20 mm in ma. Confirmed diagnosis: Schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Schwannoma.

The main symptom described in classic AINS is the partial or full disappearance of pinch grip between the thumb and index finger, usually unilaterally. Loss of PQ strength is more difficult to notice. AIN is a motor nerve, so no sensory alterations occur. Prodromal pain in the shoulder, arm, or elbow may be present. The aetiologies of anatomical compression, physical exertion, repetitive activity, infection, vaccination, pregnancy, supracondylar humerus fracture on children, sleeping on an arm, forearm immobilization, and surgery unrelated to AIN (e.g., shoulder arthroscopy) have been described, but sometimes there is no apparent cause.

There is limited evidence and no strong recommendation for the use of antiplatelet agents or long-term anticoagulation therapy in RP management. However, short-term low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) anticoagulation may be used in specific cases of acute limb ischemia. A single placebo-controlled study by Denton et al. involving 30 patients showed that LMWH reduced the severity of RP symptoms, but this finding has not been replicated in other studies.

Presentation: An 8-year-old girl arrived with a sudden onset of numbness in her right limbs, accompanied by a headache and vomiting. This was followed by tonic-clonic seizures and a subsequent loss of consciousness. Upon admission, she was found to be somnolent and moderately dehydrated, exhibiting right-sided hemiparesis and hemihypoesthesia. The temperature of her right limbs was reduced, although the pulse in her peripheral arteries remained normal.. Confirmed diagnosis: arterial thoracic outlet syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: arterial thoracic outlet syndrome.

Presentation: A 66-year-old man presented with a 15-year history of neck, supraclavicular, and right shoulder pain, along with numbness and weakness in the right arm. He underwent C3–6 posterior decompression with laminoplasty and internal fixation, followed by lumbar dynamic transpedicle fixation for lumbar disc herniation 6 months later. Post-surgery, he was unable to walk without assistance, and there was minimal improvement in arm weakness and numbness. Physical examination showed muscle weakness (Lovett grade 2/5) in the intrinsic muscles of the right hand, decreased grasp strength, and significantly reduced sensation in the ulnar part of the forearm. A positive Adson test result and minor muscle atrophy of the thenar muscles were observed. Arm abduction was limited to 30°, preventing full conduction of the Wright and Roos tests. In the Adson test posture, slight C-8 radiculopathy was noted. Electrodiagnostic studies demonstrated lower trunk axonal loss.. Confirmed diagnosis: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

The consensus process arrived at a two‐step GLIM procedure that starts with nutrition screening followed by diagnostic assessment for confirmation of malnutrition. In patients identified as being at risk of malnutrition, all five GLIM criteria should be assessed to confirm the presence of malnutrition. Three phenotypic and two etiologic criteria were selected from existing widely accepted approaches to diagnosis. All chosen criteria are well‐established nutrition‐related variables that, in their own capacity, have well‐validated prognostic value for negative clinical outcomes—ie, mortality. The three phenotypic criteria are nonvolitional weight loss, low body mass index (BMI), and low muscle mass, whereas the two etiologic criteria are reduced food intake/food assimilation and disease burden/inflammation. To confirm a malnutrition diagnosis, at least one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion must be present. Still, in occasional cases, it will not be possible to assess all five criteria. When assessment of one or more criteria is not possible for compelling practical reasons, the diagnosis of malnutrition will still be possible if, among those available, one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion are fulfilled. For exclusion of the diagnosis, all five criteria need to be assessed. Further, the severity grading of malnutrition is based solely on the phenotypic criteria. When the criteria assessment confirms the diagnosis of malnutrition, the patient should undergo a comprehensive nutrition assessment, according to available resources, to establish a treatment plan. Presentation: A 60-year-old female with a three-year history of abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss presented for evaluation of worsening symptoms. Over the previous three years, she had undergone a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and colonoscopy, including intubation of the terminal ileum and random biopsies, which did not show any abnormal pathologic findings. She was initially treated for irritable bowel syndrome based on her chronic symptoms and lack of physical findings and was prescribed dicyclomine with minimal relief. After three years of her initial symptoms, she presented at our facility for a second opinion with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She denied any constipation, diarrhea, hematochezia, rectal pain, facial flushing, or tenesmus. She reported no changes in her appetite but did have a 20-pound weight loss over the last three years. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs including afebrile. Her jugular venous pressure and heart sounds were normal without S3, S4, rubs, or gallops. Abdomen was mildly tender with hypoactive bowel sounds without rebound tenderness or guarding. Neurologic examination revealed no focal defic. Confirmed diagnosis: Carcinoid Tumor. Differential diagnosis includes: Carcinoid Tumor.

Presentation: A 51-year-old male presented with intermittent epigastric pain lasting for a few weeks. He reported no weight loss or other symptoms. Physical examination and blood tests were normal. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed no abnormalities in the lumen. A contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan identified a 3.5 cm mass lateral to the duodenum, with heterogeneous ring enhancement and coarse calcifications anteriorly. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) revealed a 6 cm x 3.5 cm circumferential lesion between the first and second segments of the duodenum. The lesion was hypoechoic, homogeneous, with central necrosis and microcystic spaces, and originated from the muscularis propria of the duodenum.. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor.

Presentation: A 25-year-old female arrived at the hospital with streaky hemoptysis lasting for 5 days. She did not report breathlessness, cough, fever, chest pain, weight loss, night sweats, visual disturbances, fainting, post-meal abdominal pain, lower limb ulcers, Raynaud's phenomenon, hair loss, or photosensitivity. She mentioned experiencing bilateral lower limb claudication with a decreasing claudication distance over the past 6 months and had a history of 3 consecutive first trimester abortions. There was no family history of hypertension or renal disease. Upon admission, she was afebrile with a pulse rate of 110 beats per minute. Blood pressure readings were 176/98 mmHg in the right brachial artery and 180/94 mmHg in the left brachial artery, while lower limb blood pressure was not recordable. No bruits were heard over any vessels. Bilateral femoral pulses were weak, and popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior interosseous pulses were absent. No abdominal or other bruits were detected. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast appears to be the method of choice for the radiologic evaluation of ME and other causes of pain in the elbow joint. Usually, it is performed if the clinical picture of the disease is unclear. On T1- and T2-weighted sequences, the thickening of the CFT (from intermediate to high) indicates ME. The most characteristic finding is increased signal intensity on the T2-weighted images in the CFT area and paratendinous edema. MRI is also practical for detecting pathologic changes in tendons, including MCL.

Injury always results in pain, which ranges from mild to severe. Physical signs may be absent or may

include any combination of soft-tissue edema, erythema, warmth, point tenderness, ecchymosis,

instability, and loss of mobility.

Presentation: A 47-year-old female presented with chronic low back pain and right L5 radiculopathy. An MRI of the lumbar spine performed at an outside institution revealed a mass-like lesion at the right L5–S1 foramen. The patient was managed with analgesics over a 1-month period, resulting in partial symptom resolution. She later visited the emergency department due to persistent symptoms, where another MRI of the lumbar spine (T1 and T2 weighted sequences) was obtained. No contrast injection was performed as it is not part of the low back pain/radiculopathy investigation protocol in the emergency department.. Confirmed diagnosis: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Differential diagnosis includes: lumbar paraspinal tumoral calcinosis secondary to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

The consensus process arrived at a two‐step GLIM procedure that starts with nutrition screening followed by diagnostic assessment for confirmation of malnutrition. In patients identified as being at risk of malnutrition, all five GLIM criteria should be assessed to confirm the presence of malnutrition. Three phenotypic and two etiologic criteria were selected from existing widely accepted approaches to diagnosis. All chosen criteria are well‐established nutrition‐related variables that, in their own capacity, have well‐validated prognostic value for negative clinical outcomes—ie, mortality. The three phenotypic criteria are nonvolitional weight loss, low body mass index (BMI), and low muscle mass, whereas the two etiologic criteria are reduced food intake/food assimilation and disease burden/inflammation. To confirm a malnutrition diagnosis, at least one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion must be present. Still, in occasional cases, it will not be possible to assess all five criteria. When assessment of one or more criteria is not possible for compelling practical reasons, the diagnosis of malnutrition will still be possible if, among those available, one phenotypic and one etiologic criterion are fulfilled. For exclusion of the diagnosis, all five criteria need to be assessed. Further, the severity grading of malnutrition is based solely on the phenotypic criteria. When the criteria assessment confirms the diagnosis of malnutrition, the patient should undergo a comprehensive nutrition assessment, according to available resources, to establish a treatment plan. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy mainly affects the peripheral nervous system, which can be divided into motor and sensory nervous systems. They relay information afferently and efferently, respectively. Sensory peripheral nerves begin in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) of the spinal cord, which is more than 1 meter long in the foot (Figure 4). The peripheral nervous system is maintained and supported by glia, Schwann cells, blood vessels, and the interstitium. The sensory peripheral nervous system is composed of unmyelinated C fibers and myelinated A‐δ fibers called small‐diameter nerve fibers, and A‐β fibers called myelinated large‐diameter nerve fibers. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, various sites of the peripheral nervous system, including DRG neurons, nerve fibers, and Schwann cells, are injured (Figure 4). Pathological evaluation shows the atrophy of DRG ganglion cells, degeneration of large nerve fibers, thickness of vascular walls of intranerve fiber vessels, and loss of small nerve fibers in the epidermis. It is generally accepted that diabetic peripheral neuropathy is a retrograde neuropathy caused by metabolic factors, mainly hyperglycemia. In the early stages of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, small‐diameter nerves within the epidermis or cornea can be first reduced. Presentation: A 76-year-old male with a 2-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer (T2aN1M0) in 2017. Due to his advanced age and weakness, he received 1.7 mg/kg of pembrolizumab every 17 days. After five doses, there was a noticeable reduction in tumor size, but he developed hypothyroidism, indicated by low thyroxine and high thyroid-stimulating hormone levels. He was prescribed L-thyroxine at 50 μg/day. Following the 11th dose in the 10th month of treatment, the patient presented to the emergency department with symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, and lethargy, but without increased urination, thirst, or hunger. Ultrasonography and measurements of amylase and lipase showed no signs of pancreatitis. Laboratory tests revealed ketonuria, hyperglycemia (590.40 mg/dL [32.80 mmol/L]), negative insulin autoimmune antibodies, and some basal β cell secretion capacity (fasting C-peptide concentration of 1.42 ng/mL), though the reserved capacity was limited (C-peptide concentration of 1.67 ng/mL at 2 hours post-meal).. Confirmed diagnosis: ICI-induced brittle Type 1 diabetes mellitus. Differential diagnosis includes: ICI-induced brittle Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

In the original consensus publication, there remained uncertainties as how to assess the phenotypic criterion on low muscle mass and the etiologic criterion on inflammation/high disease burden. Two GLIM working groups have since provided more detailed guidance; ie, calf circumference may be considered in the absence of machine‐based techniques to evaluate muscle mass, and clinical judgment of inflammatory disease burden may only require laboratory confirmation (by CRP) in cases of uncertainty. For the phenotypic criteria of nonvolitional weight loss and low BMI, no new data justify any changes from the original recommendations.

Presentation: A 62-year-old female patient with a history of total bilateral thyroidectomy and atrial fibrillation was referred to our hospital. In 2005, she was diagnosed with T2D, presenting with a hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) of 8%, and initially treated with metformin, followed by insulin. Due to inadequate hyperglycemia control, she underwent a gastric transit bipartition operation. Preoperative laboratory results showed an HbA1c level of 8.4%, fasting glucose level of 165 mg/dL, and a BMI of 41.5 kg/m2. All hypoglycemic agents were discontinued during the procedure. On the seventh postoperative day, the patient experienced frequent hypoglycemia, primarily during fasting, with glucose levels ranging from 40-45 mg/dL. After symptom improvement, she was discharged. Four months post-discharge, she reported recurrent hypoglycemia and was managed with dietary treatment for late dumping syndrome. Despite dietary adjustments, hypoglycemia persisted, leading to a planned reversal operation for PBH. Six months post-initial surgery, a cocoon formation was observed in the ileal loop from the gastrojejunostomy to the jejunojejunostomy anastomosis, which was subsequently removed, restoring normal anatomy. The. Confirmed diagnosis: Insulinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Insulinoma.

Classically, patients with an insulinoma present with fasting hypoglycemia. However, this is neither sensitive nor specific, as 20% may also experience postprandial hypoglycemia. Patients may report weight gain, as insulin has anabolic properties and inhibits lipolysis and glycogenolysis. Biochemical evidence of endogenous insulin-mediated hypoglycemia is crucial, and a supervised 72 h fast is usually recommended as a standard diagnostic step. Of note, it is helpful to know that 95% of patients with insulinoma meet end-of-fast criteria by 48 h, but the fast may be extended to 72 h as 7% of patients with proven insulinomas developed hypoglycemia after 48 h. Once endogenous insulin-mediated hypoglycemia is uncovered, localization with endoscopic ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality, due to its high sensitivity (81%) and specificity (90%). Localization can be challenging, as size and tumor behavior are factors that need to be considered. Approximately 30% of insulinomas are <1 cm and, as noted above, a small percentage can be multifocal. As indolent insulinomas tend to express GLP-1Rs, this may be used to the clinician’s advantage, and GLP-1R PET scans have reasonably high sensitivity and specificity (87% and 94%, respectively). In contrast, aggressive insulinomas preferentially express somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) instead of GLP-1R, and, in such cases, SSTR-SPECT scans may be utilized.

The most common symptoms of DM are those of hyperglycemia: an osmotic diuresis caused by

glycosuria leading to urinary frequency, polyuria, and polydipsia that may progress to orthostatic

hypotension and dehydration. Severe dehydration causes weakness, fatigue, and mental status changes.

Symptoms may come and go as plasma glucose levels fluctuate. Polyphagia may accompany symptoms

of hyperglycemia but is not typically a primary patient concern. Hyperglycemia can also cause weight

loss, nausea and vomiting, and blurred vision, and it may predispose to bacterial or fungal infections.

Patients with type 1 DM typically present with symptomatic hyperglycemia and sometimes with diabetic

ketoacidosis (DKA—. Some patients experience a long but transient phase of near-normal

glucose levels after acute onset of the disease (honeymoon phase) due to partial recovery of insulin

secretion.

Patients with type 2 DM may present with symptomatic hyperglycemia but are often asymptomatic, and

their condition is detected only on routine testing. In some patients, initial symptoms are those of diabetic

complications, suggesting that the disease has been present for some time. In some patients,

hyperosmotic coma occurs initially, especially during a period of stress or when glucose metabolism is

further impaired by drugs, such as corticosteroids.

Presentation: A 59-year-old man, who does not have diabetes, experienced sudden mental confusion, speech difficulty, and uncoordinated movements. He was evaluated at home by the emergency team. The patient appeared pale and sweaty, with normal blood pressure. A hemoglucotest revealed hypoglycemia at 31 mg/dL. Oral glucose administration normalized blood sugar levels to 106 mg/dL, resolving the symptoms. The patient was then taken to the emergency department, where he was alert and asymptomatic. Hemoglucotest showed slight hyperglycemia at 127 mg/dL, confirmed by blood tests at 166 mg/dL. Blood tests also indicated increased creatinine levels at 2.7 mg/dL (normal range 0.1-1.2), with a glomerular filtration rate of 25 mL/min. Hemogasanalysis showed no metabolic acidosis. An electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, while a chest X-ray was normal. The patient was admitted to the Internal Medicine ward. His medical history included hypertension treated with irbesartan plus hydrochlorothiazide and polycystic kidney disease with secondary stage-3 chronic kidney disease. He was also on calcitriol for secondary hyperparathyroidism and denied taking any drugs th. Confirmed diagnosis: Insulinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Insulinoma.

Chronic hyperglycemia plays an inhibitory effect on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. In bone metabolism processes, sex hormones play an important role. There is no consensus on the effect of androgens on blood glucose. Studies have reported that a large number of patients with type 2 diabetes will develop decreased testosterone. It is also believed that a lower testosterone level is an independent risk factor for the occurrence of type 2 diabetes, while a higher level of testosterone can have a preventive effect on type 2 diabetes. However, studies in women have shown that increasing total testosterone with calculated free testosterone levels is associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. There are theories calculated that androgen levels are associated with more severe insulin resistance, but the mechanisms are unclear. There is some speculation that this is related to adipocyte dysfunction. Not only the specific role and mechanism of androgens are unclear, but the relationship between estrogen and insulin resistance is not elucidated. Some studies suggest a positive relationship between estradiol and insulin resistance in women, but not in men. Another part of the studies held the exact opposite result. However, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) was inversely associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes in both men and women. A meta-analysis of sex hormones and type 2 diabetes showed gender differences in the association between testosterone and type 2 diabetes. If surgery is not an option, because of contraindications, advanced disease or patient’s preference, several palliative drug therapies have been discovered that aim to slow down the progression of the tumor. Most commonly used are the SSAs, which include mainly first generation SSAs octreotide and lanreotide, and more recently the second generation SSA pasireotide. The mechanism of action entails an endogenous inhibition of the release of glucagon, thus resulting in smaller concentrations, decreased activity and related symptom relief. In addition, the CLARINET and PROMID trials revealed better survival rates and potential slight tumor shrinkage, but only the former study included pNETs. SSAs are generally well-tolerated and safe; nonetheless, adverse effects have been documented, including diarrhea, abdominal pain, cholelithiasis, tachyphylaxis phenomena and rebound hypersecretion upon treatment pause. According to the recent guidelines SSAs, together with nutritional support, are considered first-line palliative treatment, whereas short-acting SSAs can also be given preoperatively to control symptoms. Besides nutritional support with supplementation of amino acids, zinc and fatty acids, topical dermatological therapy—and perhaps insulin or blood glucose lowering agents for a more rapid hyperglycemia resolution—may be added on occasion. Finally, the treatment plan needs to encompass the preoperative administration of low-dose heparin for DVT prevention.

Another study looked at how different pancreatic diseases (pancreatic cancer, pancreatitis, and benign tumors of the pancreas) affected glucose homeostasis and insulin secretion after a 50% partial pancreatectomy. While glucose concentrations can paradoxically improve after pancreatic head resection, the authors found that insulin secretion decreased following tail and head pancreatic resection. Obesity and glucose levels prior to surgery were risk factors for DM and hyperglycemia following pancreatic surgery. Other groups appear to agree that, in addition to beta cell reduction, the worsening of glucose control following surgery may be caused by uncontrolled or undiagnosed diabetes mellitus prior to surgery. On the other hand, as previously commented, in some cases they observed an improvement in glycemic control after pancreatic cancer resection which, they attribute to insulin resistance caused by the tumor itself or even to the weight loss induced by the failure of exocrine function, which could increase peripheral insulin sensitivity. However, only large pancreatectomies can determine malabsorption due to diminished pancreatic exocrine function, which is generally well controlled by the rapid introduction of replacement therapy with pancreatic enzymes; thus, the improvement in glycemic control observed in certain patients after pancreatectomy shows contradictory results.

Presentation: A five-year-old female, recently migrated from Africa, presented with a persistent scalp infection and otitis media. She exhibited symptomatic hyperglycemia, with a history potentially extending back to the age of two. Physical examination revealed distinct cutaneous and facial features. Laboratory tests confirmed biochemical insulin resistance, with a fasting plasma insulin level of 1836 pmol/L (normal range: 9–80 pmol/L). At the age of six, she was found to have diabetes mellitus characterized by daytime postprandial hyperglycemia and paradoxical nocturnal fasting hypoglycemia.. Confirmed diagnosis: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome.

or ethylene glycol poisoning, or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In patients

methanol and ethylene glycol levels should be obtained. Ca oxalate crystals in the urine also suggests

balance of reduction and oxidation reactions in the liver.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and Type 3 diabetes mellitus (T3DM) each have distinct characteristics. T1DM is an autoimmune disease in which the body’s immune system attacks and destroys the insulin-producing β-cells in the pancreas, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. In healthy individuals, insulin is produced in response to elevated blood glucose levels after eating, facilitating glucose uptake into cells for energy and storage. In T1DM, the lack of insulin prevents glucose absorption, resulting in hyperglycemia and inadequate cellular energy supply. The primary feature of T2DM is insulin resistance, where the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin. Over time, the pancreas may become unable to produce enough insulin to overcome this resistance. In T2DM, insulin resistance means that cells do not respond efficiently to insulin, and the pancreas struggles to meet the body’s insulin demands, leading to the accumulation of glucose in the bloodstream and the development of hyperglycemia. "T3DM" is a term used in research to describe insulin resistance in the brain, which is associated with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) but has not yet been applied clinically. In a healthy brain, insulin plays a critical role in regulating brain functions, including memory, cognition, and synaptic plasticity. However, in AD, insulin receptors (InsR) are disrupted by β-amyloid oligomers (AβO), impairing normal insulin signaling. excerpts.text: Ruling out gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) when diagnosing upper abdominal pain requires a surprising amount of anatomical knowledge. The pathophysiology of GERD is due to regurgitation of gastric acid into the distal esophagus, producing heartburn. Atypical presentations include dysphagia, esophageal bleeding, coughing, asthma, chronic laryngitis, hoarseness, dental erosion, belching, and bloating. Given its vague symptomatology, rarer conditions are often misdiagnosed as GERD, resulting in iatrogenesis. Since specialist-level knowledge of all rare conditions, with GERD among their differential diagnoses, is impractical, physicians should at least possess an understanding of esophageal anatomy sufficient to eliminate GERD from the said differential diagnoses when appropriate. For example, esophageal trachealization, a characteristic endoscopic finding of eosinophilic esophagitis, is not among the symptoms of GERD. While a definitive diagnosis of eosinophilic esophagitis is made via histopathological examination, biopsies are not routinely performed and endoscopic findings are often missed. Failure to recognize trachealization on endoscopy constitutes an ignorance of esophageal anatomy with a negative impact on patient outcomes. A multicenter retrospective study found that diagnostic delay of eosinophilic esophagitis was associated with an increase in long-term complications, such as stricture formation, perforation, and bleeding. excerpts.text: Presentation: A 52-year-old woman presented as an outpatient after experiencing right upper quadrant pain following meals. The pain was dull, aching, sudden in onset, colicky in nature, and radiated to the right scapula. She also reported nausea and vomiting. These symptoms were exacerbated by meals, especially those high in fat. Her past medical and surgical history were unremarkable, and she reported no use of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Family history included cholecystectomies in her father at age 45 due to gallstone disease and her mother at age 39 for cholesterolosis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Gallbladder Agenesis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gallbladder Agenesis.

excerpts.text: With regard to differential diagnosis with cystic echinococcosis presenting as a unilocular cyst, CE1 is particularly relevant in endemic regions. Findings of a thick, enhancing wall with a non-enhancing necrotic center suggest the diagnosis of hepatic abscess. In contrast to liver abscess, echinococcal cysts typically do not show an enhancing rim and surrounding hyperemia unless secondarily infected. Furthermore, restricted diffusion is a hallmark of abscesses, whereas uncomplicated echinococcal cysts rarely demonstrate diffusion restriction. The clinical context provides additional clues for differential diagnosis. Acute presentation with fever, leukocytosis, or right upper quadrant pain favors hepatic abscess, whereas CE typically has an indolent course. Nevertheless, in cases of infected echinococcal cysts, the precise differentiation from liver abscess might be difficult, especially in ultrasound or CT examination. In such cases, the visualization of daughter cysts or a detached membrane, if present within a thick-walled cystic lesion in MRI, indicates an infected echinococcal cyst (Figure 26). In addition, serological tests may support the diagnosis of echinococcosis when imaging findings are equivocal. Given that management strategies differ substantially, accurate differentiation between infected CE and pyogenic liver abscess is very important. While hepatic abscesses usually require systemic antimicrobial therapy, often combined with percutaneous drainage, echinococcal cysts may be managed with antihelminthic therapy or surgical intervention.

Ruling out gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) when diagnosing upper abdominal pain requires a surprising amount of anatomical knowledge. The pathophysiology of GERD is due to regurgitation of gastric acid into the distal esophagus, producing heartburn. Atypical presentations include dysphagia, esophageal bleeding, coughing, asthma, chronic laryngitis, hoarseness, dental erosion, belching, and bloating. Given its vague symptomatology, rarer conditions are often misdiagnosed as GERD, resulting in iatrogenesis. Since specialist-level knowledge of all rare conditions, with GERD among their differential diagnoses, is impractical, physicians should at least possess an understanding of esophageal anatomy sufficient to eliminate GERD from the said differential diagnoses when appropriate. For example, esophageal trachealization, a characteristic endoscopic finding of eosinophilic esophagitis, is not among the symptoms of GERD. While a definitive diagnosis of eosinophilic esophagitis is made via histopathological examination, biopsies are not routinely performed and endoscopic findings are often missed. Failure to recognize trachealization on endoscopy constitutes an ignorance of esophageal anatomy with a negative impact on patient outcomes. A multicenter retrospective study found that diagnostic delay of eosinophilic esophagitis was associated with an increase in long-term complications, such as stricture formation, perforation, and bleeding. Yet another example of a rare condition frequently misdiagnosed as GERD is achalasia, with 20-50% of cases initially misdiagnosed. Endosco
