In contrast to liver abscess, echinococcal cysts typically do not show an enhancing rim and surrounding hyperemia unless secondarily infected. Furthermore, restricted diffusion is a hallmark of abscesses, whereas uncomplicated echinococcal cysts rarely demonstrate diffusion restriction. The clinical context provides additional clues for differential diagnosis. Acute presentation with fever, leukocytosis, or right upper quadrant pain favors hepatic abscess, whereas CE typically has an indolent course. Nevertheless, in cases of infected echinococcal cysts, the precise differentiation from liver abscess might be difficult, especially in ultrasound or CT examination. In such cases, the visualization of daughter cysts or a detached membrane, if present within a thick-walled cystic lesion in MRI, indicates an infected echinococcal cyst (Figure 26). In addition, serological tests may support the diagnosis of echinococcosis when imaging findings are equivocal. Given that management strategies differ substantially, accurate differentiation between infected CE and pyogenic liver abscess is very important. While hepatic abscesses usually require systemic antimicrobial therapy, often combined with percutaneous drainage, echinococcal cysts may be managed with antihelminthic therapy or surgical intervention.

Presentation: An 18-year-old female with a history of autoimmune hepatitis and triple positive antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) on anticoagulation therapy with acenocoumarol presented to the emergency room with acute abdominal pain. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. No signs of ascites or hepatic encephalopathy were observed. Upon admission, renal and liver biochemical profiles were within normal limits. Her international normalized ratio (INR) was 4.8 while on a vitamin K antagonist, corresponding to a Child-Pugh classification of 7 points (B), considering the INR range under acenocoumarol. Abdominal Doppler ultrasonography revealed a 6 cm thrombus extending from the IVC to near the entrance of the right atrium, confirmed by computed tomography scan, with extension to all the three supra-hepatic veins. Effective collateral venous circulation was present through the lumbar and azygos veins.. Confirmed diagnosis: Budd-Chiari Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Budd-Chiari Syndrome.

Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration and core biopsy of the left hepatic lesion were inconclusive. Further tests revealed a positive Echinococcal IgG antibody, and she was started on Albendazole. After completing the therapy, she was scheduled for a complete left lateral hepatic resection. However, she returned several weeks later with worsening right upper quadrant pain. Re. A slowly progressing type of perinatal HPP, with only some or none of the skeletal abnormalities considered characteristic of HPP, may also present prenatally. This phenotype of HPP is relatively mild at birth, with some patients presenting with long bone bowing, femoral or humeral angulation, and presumed in utero fractures but no other radiologic features of HPP (Figs. 9, 10 and 11). Bone ossification is usually normal or only slightly reduced on US examinations, and chest size is usually normal. In such cases, the diagnosis of HPP may be suspected based on family history (e.g., dental abnormalities) or diagnosed after confirmation of low alkaline phosphatase activity. These patients have a better prognosis in the perinatal period than patients with perinatal or infantile HPP, which may be fatal.

Presentation: A 19-year-old female high school student presented with abnormal liver function for 2 years and was admitted to the hospital on October 17, 2018. Initially, she was found to have elevated alkaline phosphatase and γ-GT levels during a physical examination, despite being asymptomatic. Her liver function showed slight improvement after taking liver-protective medications (Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Bicyclol) as an outpatient. However, follow-up liver function tests remained abnormal. Due to her busy schedule and lack of symptoms, she initially refused hospitalization. Upon revisiting the hospital outpatient clinic on October 17, 2018, she was admitted after liver ultrasonography indicated cirrhosis. Upon admission, she exhibited no jaundice, pruritus, asthenia, anorexia, or other discomforts. She reported no history of alcohol intake or use of hepatotoxic drugs and had no family history of liver disease. Physical examination revealed mild splenomegaly, with other findings being unremarkable. Laboratory data from October 18, 2018, showed alanine aminotransferase at 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 45 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 300 U/L, γ-GT at 119 U/L, total bilirubin at 14.9 μmol. Confirmed diagnosis: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3. Differential diagnosis includes: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3.

Presentation: An 87-year-old woman presented with an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 714 U/L. The patient was asymptomatic but reported experiencing fatigue over the past few weeks. PHPT can present in many forms. The classic presentation involves elevations in both calcium and parathyroid hormone. Variants such as normo-calcemic hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia with inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone are common as well, with some studies suggesting these variants affect approximately 16% and 7% of patients presenting for evaluation of PHPT, respectively. Surgery is currently the definitive treatment of choice for preventing long-term complications of PHPT. For patients who are not surgical candidates, pharmacological management may be undertaken to address symptoms such as osteoporosis by utilizing bisphosphonates to improve bone mineral density and cinacalcet to improve serum calcium levels. The landscape of PHPT diagnosis has changed dramatically over the last few decades, with progression from ultrasound and sestamibi scans to evaluation with four-dimensional CT imaging and (11)C-choline or (18)F-choline PET/CT.

Major stimuli for the synthesis of PTH in the parathyroid glands are hypocalcemia, low 1,25(OH)2D levels, and hyperphosphatemia, whereas hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia suppress PTH levels (Fig. 4). PTH levels are markedly increased in untreated patients with calcipenic rickets in order to maintain normal serum calcium levels (Table 1). By contrast, PTH levels are usually in the normal range in patients with phosphopenic rickets, but can be slightly elevated in patients with FGF23-driven phosphopenic rickets, as FGF23 suppresses 1,25(OH)2D levels, which in turn stimulates PTH secretion in the parathyroid glands. PTH levels are often suppressed in patients with HHRH, due to 1,25(OH)2D excess. Finally, PTH levels are expected to be markedly elevated in children presenting with rickets due to CKD, which is usually associated with elevated serum phosphate and creatinine levels. Monitoring of PTH is an excellent marker for the response to therapy in patients with calcipenic rickets.

She underwent resection of all four parathyroid glands, and pathological findings confirmed parathyroid hyperplasia.. Confirmed diagnosis: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1. Presentation: A 29-year-old female with no prior health issues was identified by her primary care physician to have elevated calcium levels in 2019. We currently have many anti-catabolic therapies that increase BMD and prevent fractures. These agents, however, may also have negative immune effects. Although combined anti-resorptive/anabolic therapies (i.e. denosumab or bisphosphonate plus parathyroid hormone) are promising, combined therapy increases treatment risks and limitations (e.g. the 2-year limited duration of parathyroid hormone therapy) and most involve a degree of patient burden (e.g. intravenous or subcutaneous injections or the fasting required for oral therapy). The spine BMD effects of these anti-catabolic therapies combined with progesterone deserve examination in randomized controlled trials.

Estrogen is the bone-active component of OHT acting as an anti-catabolic agent and decreasing bone resorption. ET also increases gut calcium absorption and indirectly suppresses excess parathyroid hormone production leading to fragility fracture prevention. But balanced bone resorption (catabolism) and formation (anabolism) appear optimal for preservation of adult BMD and strength. In osteoporosis treatment - since resorption and formation are coupled at the bone mineralization unit (BMU) level - it is theoretically important to facilitate both. Because of coupling, however, anti-catabolic therapies (such as estrogen, bisphosphonates, calcitonin, selective estrogen receptor modulators and denosumab) also inhibit bone anabolism. An additional bone remodeling complexity is that resorption and formation have differing in vivo time courses; resorption in human bone takes about three weeks while new bone formation in the same BMU takes at least three months.

According to Pronicka et al., resistance to parathyroid hormone may play a key role in some individuals with Fahr’s syndrome. It is manifested by a decreased phosphaturic effect of this hormone, while cAMP excretion in urine remains within a normal range. Interestingly, this response can be improved by beta-blockers, suggesting that Fahr’s syndrome may be a result of a defect of adrenergic receptors and their impaired relationship with parathyroid hormone receptors. Another biochemical abnormality observed in Fahr’s syndrome is an increased alkaline phosphatase activity in the basal ganglia of the brain, while its level in serum remains normal. These changes may promote a precipitation of insoluble calcium phosphate salts in the nervous tissue. In up to one-third of patients with Fahr’s syndrome, a close relationship between calcifications and impaired cerebral blood flow can be demonstrated. Such patients present cerebral circulatory disturbances in the form of transient ischemic attacks or strokes. Recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.10
Why the committee made the recommendations
Type of serum calcium measurement
Although no evidence was available, the committee are confident, based on their knowledge and experience, that albumin-adjusted serum calcium measurement produces an accurate indication of the amount of calcium that is active in the body. Adjusting for albumin compensates for this, and allows better identification of the active calcium that may be causing symptoms or signs.

IGF-1, secreted by the liver through the action of this hormone, stimulates the replication of osteoblastic precursors. Specifically, it activates their function in the synthesis of matrix and collagen, in addition to inhibiting their apoptosis. However, the different isoforms have different functions. excerpts.text: Major stimuli for the synthesis of PTH in the parathyroid glands are hypocalcemia, low 1,25(OH)2D levels, and hyperphosphatemia, whereas hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia suppress PTH levels (Fig. 4). PTH levels are markedly increased in untreated patients with calcipenic rickets in order to maintain normal serum calcium levels (Table 1). By contrast, PTH levels are usually in the normal range in patients with phosphopenic rickets, but can be slightly elevated in patients with FGF23-driven phosphopenic rickets, as FGF23 suppresses 1,25(OH)2D levels, which in turn stimulates PTH secretion in the parathyroid glands. PTH levels are often suppressed in patients with HHRH, due to 1,25(OH)2D excess. Finally, PTH levels are expected to be markedly elevated in children presenting with rickets due to CKD, which is usually associated with elevated serum phosphate and creatinine levels. Monitoring of PTH is an excellent marker for the response to therapy in patients with calcipenic rickets.

excerpts.text: IIH classically presents in the first year of life with typical symptoms of hypercalcaemia, including failure to thrive, weight loss, dehydration, polyuria, vomiting and lethargy. Hypercalcaemia results from intestinal hyperabsorption and is accompanied by suppressed intact PTH and hypercalciuria. Nephrocalcinosis is also observed on kidney ultrasonography in infants from a few months of age. Hypercalcaemia generally resolves before the age of three years, although nephrocalcinosis and persistent hypercalciuria can continue to be common. Individuals with IIH may have elevated levels of serum 1,25(OH)2D3, although some have inappropriately normal levels.

In children, a diagnosis of XLH should be considered in the presence of clinical, biochemical, or radiological signs of rickets, impaired growth velocity, and hypophosphatemia associated with isolated renal phosphate wasting and in the absence of vitamin D or calcium deficiency, especially in the case of a positive family history. In patients with a negative family history (20–30% of patients), genetic testing is necessary to differentiate from other forms of hypophosphatemic rickets. A targeted panel of genes sequenced by next-generation sequencing is recommended first. However, it should be noted that some patients may have specific molecular genetic defects, such as large deletions, deletions that remove pseudo-exons of PHEX, or mosaicism.

In XLH, FGF23 levels are elevated because of loss-of-function mutations in the PHEX gene. Although the exact pathogenic mechanism remains unclear, PHEX inactivation may lead to increased FGF23 expression, potentially mediated by extracellular matrix proteins such as MEPE. This contrasts with autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets (ADHR), in which FGF23 elevation is attributed primarily to impaired degradation. However, despite being an enzyme, the expression rather than the degradation of FGF23 seems to be affected. In TIO, FGF23-producing mesenchymal tumors secrete excessive amounts of FGF23. Therefore, increased levels of FGF23 may suggest these conditions. However, in some cases, FGF23 values may appear within normal ranges, which should not be interpreted in isolation. In patients with XLH, these values may be inappropriately normal or nonsuppressed, which contrasts with the presence of hypophosphatemia and reflects an alteration in the regulation of calcium–phosphorus metabolism. High values may also be associated with hypophosphatemia due to decreased renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate and reduced synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in renal diseases. Other factors influencing FGF23 concentration include sample stability, analytical interference, the use of certain medications (in which FGF23 is not a reliable marker of treatment efficacy), and genetic mutations. Although higher FGF23 concentrations have been observed in older adults, this association is attributable primarily to an age-related decline in renal function (Table 2).

PTHrP increases the reabsorption of calcium and excretion of phosphorus in the kidneys, which results in high calcium levels in serum with simultaneous hypophosphatemia. PTHrP also causes elevated urinary cyclic AMP excretion. Besides the effect on kidneys, PTHrP can influence calcium homeostasis by its metabolic impact on bones. In bone-metastatic tumors and multiple myeloma, PTHrP is produced locally without an overall increase in serum level. By binding to the PTHR1 receptor on osteoblasts, PTHrP enhances the release of RANKL (receptor activator of factor κB ligand). RANKL then binds to the RANK receptor (Receptor Activator for Nuclear Factor κB) on osteoclasts. This molecular interaction intensifies the maturation of osteoclasts, which results in bone resorption and elevates calcium concentration. The process of bone resorption causes the secretion of growth factors such as transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), and insulin-like growth factor (IGF) 1 and 2, which stimulate the growth of the metastatic tumor. Moreover, TGF-β via activation of SMAD (suppressor of mothers against decapentaplegic) complexes and GLI2 (transcription factor Gli2) increase PTHrP transcription. This mechanism is known as a vicious cycle of bone destruction.

Upon ED presentation, she was hospitalized for pancreatitis, with findings of pancreatic duct dilation and cholelithiasis without cholecystitis, and was treated with intravenous (IV) antibiotics and analgesia. At discharge, her serum calcium was 8.6 mg/dL (2.15 mmol/L; normal range 8.5-10.5 mg/dL [2.12-2.62 mmol/L]) and she was discharged on her home hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) 25 mg daily. One month later, she returned with abdominal pain and vomiting, and was admitted for severe hypercalcemia (18.3 mg/dL; 4.57 mmol/L), hypophosphatemia, and acute kidney injury. The hypercalcemia was linked to volume contraction, vomiting, and HCTZ use. She was treated with IV fluids, calcitonin, and zoledronate. She became hypocalcemic (7.0 mg/dL; 1.75 mmol/L) and was discharged. Confirmed diagnosis: Williams Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Williams Syndrome.

Phosphate, an essential mineral in the human body, plays a pivotal role in various physiological processes, such as the regulation of acid‒base balance and bone health. Phosphate levels below normal, defined as hypophosphatemia, affect 5 to 30% of adults, depending on the setting and population. There is no universal consensus on laboratory thresholds for hypophosphatemia; however, it is generally defined as a serum phosphate concentration below 0.8 mmol/L (≈2.5 mg/dL). Moderate hypophosphatemia is usually considered between 0.32–0.64 mmol/L (≈1.0–2 mg/dL), while severe hypophosphatemia is defined as < 0.32 mmol/L (≈1.0 mg/dL). Hypophosphatemia can result from inadequate dietary intake, excessive loss through the gastrointestinal tract or kidneys, or shifts of phosphate into cells, as observed in refeeding syndrome or acute respiratory alkalosis. Excessive loss can occur due to elevated levels of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23), which impairs phosphate reabsorption in the kidneys and reduces phosphate absorption in the intestines, as observed in conditions such as X-linked hypophosphatemia and tumor-induced osteomalacia. Additionally, certain medications, such as certain iron infusions or chemotherapeutic drugs, may contribute to phosphate depletion. In case of iron infusions, this also seems to be caused by high FGF-23.

Acute hypophosphatemia can be caused by an intracellular shift, such as with hyperventilation or treatment of ketoacidosis with insulin. These shifts correct themselves and do not usually require treatment. Several studies on diabetic ketoacidosis have failed to show a benefit of phosphate supplementation; however, no such studies exist in other states, such as hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome or alcoholic ketoacidosis. Nevertheless, some authors recommend phosphate testing during treatment of the aforementioned states to detect and supplement severe (< 0.32 mmol/L; < 1 mg/dL) and/or symptomatic hypophosphatemia. A further publication recommended testing phosphate in patients with COPD or asthma due to potential hyperventilation causing a phosphate shift, especially when patients present in an exacerbated state that fails to improve despite adequate therapy. It is also well known that hypophosphatemia is common in ventilated patients and is associated with difficulties in weaning, but as we decided to exclude the ICU setting, this is outside the scope of this review. Overall, in cases of severe hypophosphatemia (< 0.32 mmol/L; < 1 mg/dL) or moderate symptomatic (e.g., altered mental status, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia, respiratory distress), supplementation is commonly recommended, with intravenous doses of 0.3–0.6 mmol (9–18 mg)/kg/day administered over 4–12 h, with laboratory monitoring after 6–24 h, although these recommendations mostly rely on case reports and expert opinions. The potential side effects of intravenous supplementation are hypocalcemia and arrhythmias;

Presentation: A 69-year-old man of Indian descent, residing in the Netherlands since 1975, presented with worsening upper abdominal pain, increasing diarrhea, and an 11 kg weight gain over two weeks. His medical history includes sarcoidosis, psoriasis, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he was alert with stable vital signs. Notable findings included severe peripheral edema, hyperpigmentation, alopecia, and nail dystrophy. Persistent pruritus was noted, previously linked to iron deficiency. Abdominal palpation was painful without rebound tenderness. Laboratory results revealed microcytic anemia (Hb 12.3 g/dL, MCV 75.8), hypoalbuminemia (20 g/L), low corrected calcium (1.44 mmol/L), hypophosphatemia (0.32 mmol/L), and hypomagnesemia (0.47 mmol/L). Elevated fecal alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance was recorded (400 mg/dL). White blood cell count, C-reactive protein, and kidney and liver function tests were within normal limits. No proteinuria was detected. Fecal and blood cultures were negative.. Confirmed diagnosis: Cronkhite-Canada syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Cronkhite-Canada syndrome.

A slowly progressing type of perinatal HPP, with only some or none of the skeletal abnormalities considered characteristic of HPP, may also present prenatally. This phenotype of HPP is relatively mild at birth, with some patients presenting with long bone bowing, femoral or humeral angulation, and presumed in utero fractures but no other radiologic features of HPP (Figs. 9, 10 and 11). Bone ossification is usually normal or only slightly reduced on US examinations, and chest size is usually normal. In such cases, the diagnosis of HPP may be suspected based on family history (e.g., dental abnormalities) or diagnosed after confirmation of low alkaline phosphatase activity. These patients have a better prognosis in the perinatal period than patients with perinatal or infantile HPP, which may be fatal.

Presentation: A 19-year-old female high school student presented with abnormal liver function for 2 years and was admitted to the hospital on October 17, 2018. Initially, she was found to have elevated alkaline phosphatase and γ-GT levels during a physical examination, despite being asymptomatic. Her liver function showed slight improvement after taking liver-protective medications (Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Bicyclol) as an outpatient. However, follow-up liver function tests remained abnormal. Due to her busy schedule and lack of symptoms, she initially refused hospitalization. Upon revisiting the hospital outpatient clinic on October 17, 2018, she was admitted after liver ultrasonography indicated cirrhosis. Upon admission, she exhibited no jaundice, pruritus, asthenia, anorexia, or other discomforts. She reported no history of alcohol intake or use of hepatotoxic drugs and had no family history of liver disease. Physical examination revealed mild splenomegaly, with other findings being unremarkable. Laboratory data from October 18, 2018, showed alanine aminotransferase at 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 45 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 300 U/L, γ-GT at 119 U/L, total bilirubin at 14.9 μmol. Confirmed diagnosis: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3. Differential diagnosis includes: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3.

Presentation: A 63-year-old male with a medical history including obesity, sleep apnea, hyperlipidemia, vitamin D deficiency, and stroke presented with persistent multifocal bone pain. He had a left hip arthroplasty for primary osteoarthritis in October 2018. Eight months post-surgery, he experienced two months of atraumatic right hip pain. MRI revealed hyperintense bone marrow edema in the intertrochanteric region and lesser trochanter, indicating a non-displaced intertrochanteric stress fracture, for which he underwent open reduction internal fixation (ORIF). Laboratory tests showed mild secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH 71 pg/mL, normal <64 pg/mL; calcium 8.5 mg/dL) and elevated alkaline phosphatase (174 U/L, normal 30–115 U/L), likely due to the fracture. Six weeks later, he was found to have a history of vitamin D deficiency and started on aggressive vitamin D supplementation. Secondary hyperparathyroidism resolved, but bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BSAP) remained elevated (67.3 μg/L, normal 7.6–14.9 μg), attributed to post-operative bone healing. Six months later, osteopenia was diagnosed, and weekly alendronate was initiated. A bone scan showed diffuse increased uptake in the proxi. Confirmed diagnosis: Phosphaturic Mesenchymal Tumor causing Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia. Differential diagnosis includes: Phosphaturic Mesenchymal Tumor causing Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia.

Presentation: A 63-year-old male patient presented with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels (ALP) of 143 IU/L (25-100 IU/L) and elevated intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) of 149.5 pg/ml (10-65 pg/ml), with normal vitamin D3 levels. Family history noted hyperlipidemia. The patient was a former smoker who quit 20 years ago and consumed alcohol occasionally. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination showed no abnormalities. Further blood work revealed elevated serum bone alkaline phosphatase at 60.2 IU/L, low serum calcium at 8 mg/dl (8.4-10.2 mg/dl), and normal levels for other isoenzymes. Other laboratory tests, including comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), glycate. Confirmed diagnosis: Celiac Disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Celiac Disease.

The hepatic involvement in sarcoidosis, more frequent in the African American male population, is most often asymptomatic and can manifest only with hepatomegaly and, in 10% of cases, with an increase of transaminases and alkaline phosphatase.

Presentation: A 58-year-old Tunisian woman with a history of arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus was admitted due to a 20 kg weight loss, dyspnoea, dry cough, and back pain persisting for two years. Presentation: A 23-year-old woman of Asian Indian origin was admitted to the orthopedic emergency department with pain in her left shoulder, right knee, and left thigh following a minor trauma. Laboratory results showed serum calcium at 11.4 mg/dl (normal 8.4-10.7 mg/dl), serum albumin at 5 g/dl (normal 3.4-4.8 g/dl), serum alkaline phosphatase at 780 IU/l (normal 50-240 IU/l), serum acid phosphatase at 11.36 IU/l (normal 0-5.5 IU/l), serum parathyroid hormone at 456 pg/ml (normal 7-53 pg/ml), vitamin D3 (1,25-dihydroxy cholecalciferol) at 32 pg/ml (normal 25-45 pg/ml), and vitamin D3 (25-hydroxy cholecalciferol) at 37 ng/ml (normal 15-80 ng/ml). Presentation: An 87-year-old woman presented with an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 714 U/L. The patient was asymptomatic but reported experiencing fatigue over the past few weeks. She denied abdominal pain, loss of appetite, pruritus, or weight loss. The patient had allergies to atorvastatin, lisinopril, irbesartan, and montelukast. Her medical history included recurrent nodular malignant melanoma with metastasis to the left pelvis and bilateral femurs, for which she had undergone wide total excision and left inguinal lymph node resection. She also had type 2 diabetes, essential hypertension, hypothyroidism, and rheumatoid arthritis. Vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed bilateral lower-extremity edema up to the thighs, but no abdominal distention, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses, and the liver span was normal. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal red and white blood cell and platelet counts, with hemoglobin and hematocrit levels within normal limits, as well as a normal coagulation profile. Serum transaminases, albumin, and globulin levels were within normal limits, except for elevated alkaline phosphatase at 714 . Confirmed diagnosis: AMA-negative Primary Biliary Cholangitis. Differential diagnosis includes: AMA-negative Primary Biliary Cholangitis.

Presentation: A 4-year-old boy of Arab origin was first evaluated for elevated calcium levels at the age of 9 months following an episode of febrile convulsion. Routine laboratory tests at that time revealed increased calcium levels. His parents are nonconsanguineous. He was born late preterm at 35 weeks gestation via normal vaginal delivery, with no significant postnatal complications and was discharged home after birth. His surgical history includes the repair of bilateral inguinal hernia. Family history includes congenital heart disease in the mother, specifically pulmonary stenosis treated with balloon dilatation, and a sister with PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) closed by catheterization. The mother has alpha-thalassemia trait, and the father had bilateral congenital cataract. Upon admission and further evaluation for elevated calcium levels, the patient exhibited persistent low urinary calcium to creatinine ratio adjusted for age, slightly elevated magnesium levels, normal PTH, phosphate, and vitamin D levels, and high alkaline phosphatase. The mother was also found to have elevated calcium levels, low urinary calcium, normal magnesium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase, and low vitamin D. Confirmed diagnosis: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia Type 3. Differential diagnosis includes: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia Type 3.

Also, patients with hepatocellular dysfunction or cholestasis have dark urine due to bilirubinuria because

The diagnosis should be suspected in patients with risk factors such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus,

or dyslipidemia and in patients with unexplained laboratory abnormalities suggesting liver disease. The

most common laboratory abnormalities are elevations in aminotransferase levels. Unlike in alcoholic liver

disease, the ratio of AST/ALT in NASH is usually < 1. Alkaline phosphatase

and

γ

(GGT) occasionally increase. Hyperbilirubinemia, prolongation of PT, and hypoalbuminemia are

uncommon.

For diagnosis, strong evidence (such as a history corroborated by friends and relatives) that alcohol

intake is not excessive (eg, is < 20 g/day) is needed. Serologic tests should show absence of hepatitis B

and C infection (ie, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibody should be negative). Liver

biopsy should reveal damage similar to that seen in alcoholic hepatitis, usually including large fat droplets

(macrovesicular fatty infiltration). Indications for biopsy include unexplained signs of portal hypertension

(including splenomegaly or cytopenia) and unexplained elevations in aminotransferase levels that persist

for > 6 mo in a patient with diabetes, obesity, or dyslipidemia.

Imaging tests, including ultrasonography, CT, and particularly MRI, may identify hepatic steatosis.

However, these tests cannot identify the inflammation typical of NASH and cannot differentiate NASH

from other causes of hepatic steatosis.

Hereditary disorders associated with hypercalcemia include familial isolated primary hyperparathyroidism (FIHP), familial benign hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FBHH), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), MEN type 2 (MEN2), and the hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor (HPT-JT) syndrome. The hypercalcemia of FIHP, MEN1, MEN2, and HPT-JT (Table 2) is associated with hypercalciuria and sometimes kidney stones, whereas that of FBHH is associated with a low urinary calcium–creatinine clearance ratio (< 0.01). In FBHH, which is an autosomal dominant disorder, the hypercalcemia is usually mild to moderate, i.e. within 10% of the upper limit of normal, although some patients do have more severe hypercalcemia. Other biochemical features include mild hypermagnesemia and normal or mildly elevated serum PTH concentrations. FBHH is due to inactivating mutations of the CASR gene, which is located on chromosome 3q21.1, whereas the genes causing MEN1, MEN2 and HPT-JT are located on chromosomes 11q13, 10q11.2, and 1q31.2, respectively. Some patients with FIHP have mutations of the MEN1, HPT-JT and CaSR genes, although the majority of FIHP patients do not have such mutations and the genes involved need to be characterized. Five CaSR mutations (Thr100Ile, Lys336deletion, Leu650Pro, Val689Met and Phe881Leu) have been reported in FIHP. Functional characterization of the mutant Phe881Leu CaSR only, has been undertaken in HEK293 cells, and this demonstrated that the Phe881Leu mutation resulted in a loss of function. Presentation: A male child, aged 1 year and 1 month, was admitted to the Department of Pediatric Medicine of Inner Mongolia Maternal and Child Health Hospital in June 2022 due to elevated calcium levels in the blood and gastrointestinal bleeding. Five months prior to admission, the child experienced poor weight gain despite being fed high-calorie milk powder. Three days before admission, the child presented with dark red bloody stool, lethargy, and reduced milk intake. Outpatient measurements showed a total serum calcium level of 3.98 mmol/L (reference range: 2.1–2.8 mmol/L). The child was born at term via caesarean section, with a birth weight of 2460 g, grade III amniotic fluid contamination, and the umbilical cord wrapped around the neck for 1 week. Neonatal Apgar scores were recorded at 1, 7, 5, and 9 minutes. Developmental delays were noted, with the child raising his head at 5 months. Currently, he is unable to sit or climb independently and makes sounds like 'baba' and 'mama' unconsciously. The parents are healthy, nonconsanguineous, and report no family history of hereditary disease or similar hypercalcemia. The child has a healthy 8-year-old sister. Parental blood calcium and phosphorus. Confirmed diagnosis: Williams syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Williams syndrome.

Other causes of hypercalciuria include conditions with an excessive bone resorption (prolonged immobilization, prolonged use of corticosteroids, osteolytic metastases to bone, primary hyperparathyroidism) or excessive calcium absorption from the intestines (vitamin D3 overdose, hypersensitivity to vitamin D3—including HCINF1, and granulomatous diseases, e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, leading to excessive hydroxylation of vitamin D to the active metabolite 1,25(OH)2D). Hypercalciuria also occurs in many congenital tubulopathies such as Fanconi syndrome (generalized proximal tubular damage), Dent disease (#300009,#300555), Bartter syndrome (#601678, #241200, #607364, #602522, #613090, #300971), hypocalcemic hypercalciuria, familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis (#248250, #248190), and as an effect of loop diuretics. A progressive proximal renal tubulopathy with hypercalciuria, low-molecular-weight proteinuria, and nephrocalcinosis characterizes dent disease-1 (#300009). In contrast, the characteristic abnormalities of Dent disease-2 (#300555) include low-molecular-weight proteinuria and other features of Fanconi syndrome, such as glycosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia, but typically do not include proximal renal tubular acidosis. Bartter syndrome refers to a group of disorders characterized by pronounced salt wasting (due to impaired salt reabsorption in the thick ascending loop of Henle), polyuria, dehydration, hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, hyperreninemia, normal or low blood pressure, hypercalciuria, and failure to thrive.

Despite data supporting the use of TNF-a antagonists to treat sarcoidosis, these drugs have been reported to induce sarcoid-like reactions. Etanercept was most often involved, but cases were also seen with adalimumab, infliximab, golimumab, and biosimilars. The reason for TNF-a antagonist therapy was usually rheumatoid arthritis, although some patients had ankylosing arthritis, Crohn’s disease, or even sarcoidosis. TNF-a antagonist-induced granulomatous disease is rare; thus, only four (0.57%) cases were identified among 697 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The mean duration of TNF-a antagonist exposure has varied widely, from 7 to 123 months in rheumatoid arthritis and 1 to 180 months in Crohn’s disease. Diffuse lung infiltration with or without hilar lymphadenopathy was common. Peripheral lymphadenopathy, uveitis, and involvement of the spleen, muscle, parotid glands, and spinal cord have also been reported. Laboratory test abnormalities included hypercalcemia, which was severe in some patients, and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels. Diagnostic challenges arise due to the low incidence of TNF-a antagonist-induced granulomatosis, wide variability in exposure duration at symptom onset, and possible presence of symptoms due to the underlying disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis or Crohn’s disease). Presentation: A 7-month-old male infant was admitted to our clinic. The patient was born full-term to a 41-year-old mother via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 2.900 g and measuring 51 cm in height. The parents are consanguineous (cousins). The patient had a history of multiple hospitalizations due to elevated calcium levels and had experienced several septic episodes related to prolonged hospital stays. Surgery was delayed until the patient reached a weight of 5 kg. Blood samples from the parents revealed familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia with both parents carrying two copies of the missense mutation pro39ala. Upon admission, the patient weighed 4.300 g and measured 62 cm in height. He exhibited severe respiratory distress and subcostal retractions. Lung auscultation revealed bilaterally diminished sounds, along with rales and rhonchi.. Confirmed diagnosis: Neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism. Differential diagnosis includes: Neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism.

Presentation: An 87-year-old female with a history of thyroid cancer, primary hyperparathyroidism, and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) was referred for evaluation of prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) noted during a preoperative assessment. Two months prior, she was diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer and was scheduled for a thyroidectomy the following month. Three years ago, she was identified with immunoglobulin A (IgA) MGUS during an evaluation for hypercalcemia, which was attributed to primary hyperparathyroidism. An immunofixation test conducted six months earlier showed a lower level of IgA with kappa light chain, indicating stable MGUS. The patient reported no hematuria, epistaxis, postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, or easy bruising. She had undergone previous surgeries without prolonged PT and PTT or excessive bleeding. Physical examination revealed that she was hemodynamically stable with no signs of bleeding. Laboratory workup revealed a prolonged PT, PTT, and an isolated decrease in the activity of factor X which corrected upon mixing studies.. Confirmed diagnosis: Acquired Factor X Deficiency. Differential diagnosis includes: Acquired Factor X Deficiency.

Immobilization due to fractures, burns, paralysis, or other causes is known to induce marked changes in calcium metabolism that may include hypercalcemia (>10.0 mg/dl), hypercalciuria (urinary calcium/creatinine ratio >0.3), elevated serum ionized calcium, and, if immobilization is prolonged, decreased total body calcium and loss of bone mineral density. It has been demonstrated that acute hypercalcemia during intravenous calcium infusion increases blood pressure and peripheral vascular resistance in both normotensive and hypertensive individuals. Whether or not alterations in calcium metabolism lead to immobilization-induced hypertension is less clear. Several case reports describe hypertension associated with marked hypercalcemia, although in some of these reports, comorbid conditions such as renal insufficiency may also have contributed. However, larger studies on hypertension in immobilized children have found no significant correlation between hypertension and hypercalcemia. Symptoms of hypercalcemia are nonspecific and include nausea, vomiting, constipation, seizures, and behavioral changes. If an immobilized patient develops hypertension, it is reasonable to assess serum total and ionized calcium, as ionized calcium may be elevated in immobilized patients even with normal total calcium levels.

The optimal treatment of immobilization-induced hypercalcemia has not been established. Increased fluid administration, loop diuretics, calcitonin, and bisphosphonates have all been shown to decrease serum calcium in the short term. In the long run, however, increased activity with weightbearing exercise is most effective in inducing complete resolution of hypercalcemia and hypertension.

Blood tests upon hospitalization revealed elevated levels of total calcium (3.42 mmol/L; Ref. . Confirmed diagnosis: Idiopathic Infantile Hypercalcemia due to CYP24A1 mutation. The search process used the following terms ‘c-section’, ‘C-Sections’, ‘Cesarean’, ‘Adhesions’, ‘Surgery Induced Tissue Adhesions’ and ‘sliding sign’. Studies were considered for eligibility if the population was gravida women with at least 1 prior CD, the diagnostic test was the absence of sliding sign in trans-abdominal ultrasonography, the reference test was surgical reports following CD and the outcome was existence of intra-abdominal adhesions involving the uterus. Intraabdominal adhesions in included studies involved any adhesions related to the access of the surgeons to the planned uterine incision (thin, filmy and easily separated adhesions by gentle, blunt or manual dissection with no vascular structures or adhesions between bowel or bladder and anterior uterine side making access to the lower uterine segment difficult and often require sharp dissection to release). Based on intraoperative findings, 4 levels of adhesions were identified: absent, mild (little or filmy adhesions), moderate (moderate to thick adhesions, require sharp dissection but do not involve bladder or bowel), and severe (absence of free space between uterine and abdominal walls or adhesions between uterus and bladder or bowel). A freely moving uterus indicated a low chance of adhesions (positive sliding sign). No uterine movement under the fascia of abdominal muscles suggested severe adhesions (negative sliding sign). US findings were compared to surgical reports following CD surgery as the reference standard test.

Presentation: A 10-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric chronic pain clinic due to persistent pain throughout his body, including headaches, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain, which had been ongoing for several years. The onset of pain began around the age of seven and a half, with no prior medical or surgical history. Over a few weeks, the pain spread to multiple locations including thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, muscular areas, and the head. There were no identified triggering factors. The pain episodes were frequent, almost daily, and lasted from a few seconds to five minutes. The child reported that the pain was sometimes so intense that he could not move or would drop objects. The pain did not disturb his sleep. Cardiological (electrocardiogram) and neurological (standard and prolonged electroencephalogram, brain MRI) assessments showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound and a contrast-enhanced abdomen were normal except for slight fecal impaction, which required no specific intervention. Stool analysis and lactose tolerance tests were normal. Pain management included occasional use of ibuprofen, which had limited effectiveness. At the age of 10, due to persistent pain, he wa. Confirmed diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder. Differential diagnosis includes: Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Presentation: A 66-year-old white male with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and previous open drainage of a liver abscess presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain and tenderness. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed fecal impaction and pneumatosis intestinalis in the distal descending colon. The patient was taken to the operating room for extensive lysis of liver adhesions, likely resulting from his prior liver surgery, and exploration revealed severe colonic impaction. Manual disimpaction of fecal material and gas, peritoneal irrigation, and closure were performed. Initially, his postoperative course was uneventful, and he was quickly weaned off the ventilator. Later in the evening, he experienced retrosternal chest pain described as sharp to tight, without radiation. Deep inspiration worsened his abdominal pain at the incision site but did not change the severity of his chest pain. His blood pressure and heart rate remained stable. ECG revealed inferior ST elevations with reciprocal ST depressions in the anterior leads. An echocardiogram revealed normal left and right ventricular dimensions and systolic function without obvious wall motion abnorm. Confirmed diagnosis: Regional Pericarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Regional Pericarditis.

Presentation: A 37-year-old female presented with low potassium levels identified during routine tests following abdominal surgery performed 3 years prior due to diaphragm rupture. She had no prior medical history and no specific management except for increased potassium intake in the first year after low potassium levels were detected. She experienced muscle cramps and weakness, along with low potassium levels. After a year, she was referred to a nephrologist due to worsening weakness and the development of increased urination, nighttime urination, and headaches. She was hospitalized multiple times for severe low potassium levels and weakness. During these periods, she was treated with intravenous potassium chloride and various oral medications, including spironolactone up to 500 mg per day (discontinued due to menstrual issues); eplerenone 100 mg twice daily; and potassium chloride 600 mg tablets up to 5 doses per day. Throughout all outpatient and inpatient visits, her blood pressure remained normal. There was no family history of hypertension. Her family history included diabetes mellitus in her mother, sister, and two brothers, and proteinuria in her mother, possibly related to diabetic nep. Confirmed diagnosis: Primary Hyperaldosteronism due to Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Primary Hyperaldosteronism due to Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma.

Enteroviruses are positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses encompassing multiple serotypes, including 2 specific viruses that have been associated with NEC: coxsackievirus and echovirus. These infections are seasonal, with most cases occurring during summer and fall. Among 27 infants with enterovirus, 3 had NEC marked by fevers, abdominal distention, and bloody diarrhea and one had coxsackievirus B and died following exploratory surgery revealing dusky jejunum. Another fatal case of NEC associated with widespread coxsackievirus B infection demonstrated ischemic ileum with subserosal hemorrhage; the child’s parents were both febrile at the time of birth. The clinical presentation of echovirus infection among premature infants ranges from asymptomatic to diarrheal illness to upper and lower respiratory tract infections. An outbreak of echovirus type 22 in a NICU resulted in a diarrheal illness among 12 premature infants, 6 (50%) of whom developed stage I NEC and one had pneumatosis intestinalis, but all survived. Identification of echovirus was via stool culture in most infants, though a few only had increased serum antibody titers.

Presentation: A 24-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute pain in the right lower quadrant of her abdomen and episodes of vomiting. She did not experience weight loss or diarrhea and had no prior history of abdominal surgery or allergic conditions. She also reported not using any medications or herbal remedies. Physical examination indicated tenderness and rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory tests showed a white cell count of 14,400/mm3, with 75% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 3.3% monocytes, and 4.3% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count of 619/mm3). Other laboratory results and stool tests for ova and parasites were normal. During a surgical procedure, bowel edema and a moderate amount of ascites were observed in the abdominal cavity, but there was no visible evidence of appendicitis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis with Eosinophilic Dermatitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis with Eosinophilic Dermatitis.

Presentation: A 49-year-old Caucasian woman with a medical history of type II diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and hypertension presented to the emergency department with cramping abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea that began a few weeks prior. The abdominal pain was initially generalized and later localized to the epigastrium without radiation. There were no alleviating or aggravating factors. She experienced frequent, watery to loose, non-bloody bowel movements. The patient denied difficulty swallowing, painful swallowing, fever, chills, skin rashes, or joint pains. She also denied recent travel, sick contacts, or antibiotic use before symptom onset. The review of systems was unremarkable. Her surgical history included a cholecystectomy. She did not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs, and there was no family history of similar symptoms. The patient was admitted for further management. Prior to this hospitalization, she had been evaluated and treated at two different healthcare facilities, including one hospital admission, for similar symptoms. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast from a previous hospital visit showed fluid-filled bowels and a thickene. Confirmed diagnosis: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis and Eosinophilic Esophagitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis and Eosinophilic Esophagitis.

The timing and type of surgery have also been observed to play a role in developing PSD. Studies have shown that sleep quality in young adults and middle-aged patients was heavily influenced by the surgical start time. Patients with surgeries that occurred in the afternoon (14:00–18:00) had increased levels of cortisol and decreased melatonin on postoperative night one than patients who underwent surgery in the morning, resulting in the afternoon group having almost twice the rate of sleep disturbances (70% of patients vs. 39%, respectively). It is believed that patients with morning surgeries may achieve better sleep due to having a recovery period that does not overlap with a sleeping period. Interestingly, these results were not observed in older patients, presumably due to their decreased metabolism, which requires longer periods of time to recover from surgery. With regards to how the type of surgery affects the development of PSDs, major surgery has been found to have a greater suppressive effect on slow wave sleep and REM sleep than minor surgery. Gögenur et al. found that sleep quality after laparoscopic surgery returned to normal values in under a week compared to major abdominal surgery sleep recovery, which took over 4 weeks. This is believed to be related to the increased levels of trauma that occur in major abdominal surgery. Additionally, major abdominal surgery usually necessitates longer hospital stays, while laparoscopic patients may be discharged from the hospital on the same day. Presentation: An 83-year-old man with a history of hypertension and asthma, and no prior abdominal surgeries, presented to the Department of General Surgery with an 8 × 8 cm necrotic area at the scrotal base. Nineteen years earlier, the patient had received radiation therapy twice over four years, totaling 82 Gy, for a condition in the same region. The patient was evaluated by colorectal surgeons, plastic surgeons, and urologists. The lesion was located at the scrotal base and featured a necrotic ulcer in the perianal area. Initial assessments considered the condition as a potential side effect of previous radiation therapy. Multiple biopsies were performed, and histopathological examination revealed specific findings without signs of invasiveness. Further clinical workup, including a normal colonoscopy and MRI of the lower abdomen, ruled out involvement of the urethra or corpora cavernosum.. Confirmed diagnosis: Primary perianal Paget’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Primary perianal Paget’s disease.

Presentation: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a typical decrease in T2-weighted signal intensity over the liver.. Confirmed diagnosis: Type 3 Hemochromatosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 3 Hemochromatosis.

Cecal volvulus: (a) Erect plain radiograph of the abdomen in a 65-year-old male patient presenting with severe abdominal pain demonstrates mildly dilated loops of small bowel (short arrows) in the right hemi abdomen and a markedly dilated gas filled structure in the left upper quadrant (long arrow) which is compressing the stomach which contains nasogastric tube. Axial contrast enhanced computed tomography images (b and c) demonstrate a large air and fluid filled structure in the left abdomen (asterisk) with absence of cecum in its normal location. A small amount of fluid (arrow) is noted secondary to early ischemia. The enteric contrast is noted to opacify only the small bowel. Imaging findings are concerning for cecal volvulus which was subsequently confirmed at surgery.

Colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction is called pseudo-obstruction and has been broadly separated into acute and chronic types, with each type having their own disease progression and management. Although there is no obstructing lesion, particularly acute colonic dilatation can be rapidly progressive leading to ischemia and perforation of the large bowel. Added to that, mistaking pseudo-obstruction for mechanical obstruction can lead to unnecessary surgery. The acute type is usually known as Ogilvie's syndrome. The exact pathogenesis of Ogilvie's is unknown, however an imbalance in autonomic nervous system activity is thought be a major contributing factor. In a review of cases, Ogilvie's most prominent symptoms are an abdominal pain (83%), constipation (51%), diarrhea (41%), fever (37%), and abdominal distention. It most often occurs in patients who are critically ill, have electrolyte imbalances, or are on anticholinergic medications. If untreated, life-threatening complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation can occur in up to 15% of cases with 50% mortality.

Presentation: A 79-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department experiencing severe epigastric pain that began suddenly 2 hours prior. The pain was constant and intense. She also felt bloated but had been passing hard bowel motions in the days leading up to the visit and had passed flatus that morning. There was no history of weight loss or rectal bleeding. Her past medical history included coronary artery disease, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and blastocystis. She had no history of abdominal surgery and was an independent, non-smoker. On physical examination, she was mildly tachypneic with normal oxygen saturation levels. Her heart rate was 74 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 151/80 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed gross distension, guarding, and signs of peritonitis throughout, with no palpable hernias. Blood tests showed an elevated white cell count of 13.4 × 10^9/l and a lactate level of 2.3 mmol/l.. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Bowel Volvulus with Chylous Ascites. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Bowel Volvulus with Chylous Ascites.

There are multiple surgical options for POP, broadly split into two categories: reconstructive and obliterative surgeries. Reconstructive surgeries maintain the vaginal canal for the purposes of penetrative intercourse and can use native tissues (when done transvaginally) or synthetic materials such as mesh (when done in a minimally invasive fashion transabdominally). For patients interested in transvaginal surgery for advanced prolapse who do not desire to maintain the vaginal canal (older, no longer sexually active), obliterative surgery (colpocleisis) is an option.

Presentation: An 11-month-old girl was brought to the emergency facility with a 7-day history of fever (maximum 38 °C), abdominal pain, irritability, and a 3-day history of constipation. The plain abdominal x-ray showed a distended large bowel and a collapsed distal colon, which are consistent with a large bowel obstruction. Therefore, a glycerin enema was performed to rule out fecal impaction. An abdominal ultrasound showed a pelvic mass with a liquid content and possible septations, which were interpreted as possible grouped intestinal loops or a cystic lesion. The abdominal computed tomography (CT) diagnosed a pelvic/hypogastric, expansive, loculated cystic lesion with lobulated contour extending to the mesogastrium, measuring 5.5 × 4.1 × 5.2 cm, with parietal enhancement after contrast infusion, displacing the intestinal loops to the right side, and compressing the sigmoid colon. The blood cell count revealed hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL (reference value [RV]: 10.5-13.5 g/dL), leukocytes of . Confirmed diagnosis: Subserous lymphangioma. Presentation: A 43-year-old man with no prior medical history came to our hospital for evaluation of anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test. Laboratory results indicated a hemoglobin level of 11.2 g/dl. Despite performing gastroscopy and colonoscopy, the source of gastrointestinal bleeding remained unidentified. The small bowel was subsequently examined using capsule endoscopy (PillCamTM SB2, Given Imaging, Yokneam, Israel). The patient was unable to pass the capsule more than 2 weeks after ingestion but did not experience pain or symptoms of bowel obstruction. An abdominal X-ray showed the capsule retained on the right side of the abdomen, and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the capsule's presence in the small bowel.. Confirmed diagnosis: Crohn's disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Crohn's disease.

Most importantly, EGDS not only allows a prompt and precise identification of the bleeding source proximal to the ligament of Treitz, but also allows timely hemostasis (see paragraph “endoscopic therapy”). Patients presenting with hematochezia and concurrent hemodynamic instability should be firstly evaluated by EGDS to exclude an upper gastrointestinal bleeding source. Otherwise, ileo-colonoscopy is recommended as the first step in the evaluation of acute LGIB, being the diagnostic yield high up to 89–97%. The optimal timing of ileo-colonoscopy after initial presentation ranges from 12 h to 48 hours. As well as EGDS, colonoscopy can determine the source and type of bleeding, and helps identifying patients with ongoing bleeding or those who are at high risk of rebleeding, moreover, allows endoscopic hemostasis if necessary. Unlikely EGDS, ileo-colonoscopy requires thorough cleansing of the colon even in acute LGIBs, to improve sensitivity and safety of the procedure by decreasing the risk of perforation. Although in urgent procedures it is not always possible, an optimal purge of the colon consists in the assumption of 3–6 litres of a polyethylene glycol-based solution, anyway patients generally tolerate consumption of 1-2 l per hour. In case of negative upper and lower endoscopy and presence of GIB, the small bowel should be investigated. Usually, the exploration of the small intestine is elective and performed by using firstly Video Capsule Endoscopy (VCE), then by performing device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) in case an operative endoscopic intervention is needed. The clinical implications of SIBO have been a subject of heated debate in the gastroenterological literature for years. The very definition of SIBO—precisely what threshold of bacterial density constitutes “overgrowth”—as well as the optimal way to diagnose this, and how such a diagnosis relates to symptoms or indeed, responds to treatment, are all areas that continue to evolve. Originally formulated as potentially injurious colonization of the small bowel by colonic bacteria in high-risk patients with evidence of malabsorption, SIBO has since been invoked as a general cause of bloating in average-risk patients and those with functional GI disorders. Symptoms attributed to SIBO in addition to bloating are abdominal pain, diarrhea, flatulence, and nutritional deficiencies. Several diseases or physiological changes are associated with SIBO, including PD, such as scleroderma or surgical alterations in GI anatomy. Although the etiology is multifactorial, small intestinal transit time has been shown to be delayed in SIBO and can occur even when gastric emptying time is normal.

Presentation: A 54-year-old male, employed as a shepherd, presented with a three-month history of intermittent colicky pain in the central abdomen, accompanied by episodes of bilious vomiting and increasing abdominal distension. For the past two weeks, he also noted the passage of linear membrane-like structures in his stools. He had no other symptoms. His medical history included surgical removal of a hepatic cyst 20 years ago. Initial evaluation at a peripheral health center suggested a possible subacute intestinal obstruction due to helminthic infestation. Upon presentation, the patient was afebrile with stable vital signs. Physical examination showed a distended, non-tender abdomen that was dull to percussion, with no fluid thrill or shifting dullness. A right subcostal scar was observed, consistent with his previous liver surgery. Auscultation indicated increased bowel sounds, while the rest of the systemic examination was normal. Hematological and biochemical tests were within normal limits.. Confirmed diagnosis: Transmural gastroduodenal fistulization of a peritoneal hydatid cyst with multiple small intraluminal cysts and membranes within the bowel, subacute small bowel obstruction, and concomitant peritoneal and retroperitoneal hydatidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Transmural gastroduodenal fistulization of a peritoneal hydatid cyst with multiple small intraluminal cysts and membranes within the bowel, subacute small bowel obstruction, and concomitant peritoneal and retroperitoneal hydatidosis.

Evaluation aims to exclude serious or life-threatening causes of nausea and vomiting. Morning sickness

(uncomplicated nausea and vomiting) and hyperemesis gravidarum are diagnoses of exclusion.

History: History of present illness

should particularly note the following:

Important associated symptoms include diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain. If pain is present, the

location, radiation, and severity should be queried. The examiner should also ask what social effects the

symptoms have had on the patient and her family (eg, whether she is able to work or to care for her

children).

Review of systems

should seek symptoms of nonobstetric causes of nausea and vomiting, including

fever or chills, particularly if accompanied by flank pain or voiding symptoms (UTI or pyelonephritis), and

neurologic symptoms such as headache, weakness, focal deficits, and confusion (migraine or CNS

hemorrhage).

Past medical history

includes questions about morning sickness or hyperemesis in past pregnancies.

Past surgical history should include questions about any prior abdominal surgery, which would predispose

a patient to mechanical bowel obstruction.

Drugs taken by the patient are reviewed for drugs that could contribute (eg, iron-containing compounds,

hormonal therapy) and for safety during pregnancy.

Physical examination begins with a review of vital signs, particularly for fever

and signs of hypovolemia (hypotension, tachycardia).

Evaluation focuses on abdominal and pelvic examinations. The abdomen is palpated for tenderness,

peritoneal signs (rebound, rigidity, guarding), and uterine size and is percussed for tympany. Fetal heart

sounds are checked using a Doppler probe.

Pelvic examination includes inspection of the cervix for discharge, dilation, and bleeding. Discharge, if

present, should be sampled and sent for culture. Any blood or clots in the vaginal vault are gently

removed. Bimanual examination should check for cervical motion tenderness, adnexal masses or

tenderness, and uterine size.

Presentation: A 42-year-old man with a history of chronic diarrhea over 2 years was admitted to our clinic. He did not report any gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, weight loss, or nocturnal diarrhea, and there was no history of food allergy or atopy. Physical examinations, including abdominal examination, were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal liver function tests. Repeated stool examinations for ova/parasites and serological tests for toxocara and strongyloides were negative. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed to evaluate for malignancy, and the results were negative. Chromosomal testing, including evaluation of BCR-ABL mutation and Jack2 mutation, was also negative. Abdominal CT and small bowel transit studies were normal. Hematological workup did not indicate any organ damage.. Confirmed diagnosis: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis. Differential diagnosis includes: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

Presentation: A 26-year-old obese Hispanic male initially presented to the ER in 2013 with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. There was no significant past surgical or social history. Family history included unknown cancer in his mother and brother. He was diagnosed with unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and discharged. Over the next five years, starting in 2018, he returned to the ED multiple times with similar symptoms and was diagnosed with fatty liver disease and gastroenteritis after an abdominopelvic CT series. Later that year, he presented with more severe pain, and workup revealed numerous ruptured jejunal ulcers, signs of peritonitis, and severe sepsis. He underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which was converted to exploratory laparotomy for small bowel resection without anastomosis. A laparotomy pad was left to pack the duodenum, and the viability at the duodenal jejunal flexure was questionable. A few days later, he had surgery for resection of the third and fourth portions of the duodenum due to necrosis, small bowel resection, gastrojejunostomy, pyloroplasty, and inse. Confirmed diagnosis: gastrinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: gastrinoma.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a condition where excessive amounts of bacteria typically found in the colon are found in the small intestine and result in various gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. Patient with IBD, particularly Crohn’s disease, are at increased risk of SIBO. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the proportion of SIBO in patients with IBD was 22.3% (95% CI 19.92–24.68). The odds ratio (OR) for SIBO in patients with IBD was 9.51 (95% CI 3.39–26.68) compared to controls without IBD. The OR was significantly elevated in both CD (OR 10.86; 95% CI 2.76–42.69) and UC (OR 7.96; 95% CI 1.66–38.35). In subgroup analysis, patients with fibrostenosing CD (OR 7.47; 95% CI 2.51–22.20) and prior bowel surgery (OR 2.38; 95% CI 1.65–3.44), had increased odds of SIBO. The underlying pathophysiology behind SIBO in IBD may be due to impaired intestinal mucosal integrity, intestinal stasis caused by strictures, and/or intra-abdominal adhesions and prior intestinal surgeries. Additionally, any structural factor that allows colonic bacteria to enter the small bowel, such as enterocolic fistulas or lack of an ileocecal valve can facilitate SIBO. The symptoms of SIBO are non-specific and non-predictive for SIBO, however commonly patients complain of bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and constipation. The preferred method to diagnose SIBO is the lactulose or glucose breath test (Table 1). The test is considered positive if there is a rise in baseline breath hydrogen by ≥ 20 by 90 min. Presentation: A 42-year-old male with a history of cervical spine injury resulting in paraplegia since adolescence and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, as well as a small bowel obstruction treated with lysis of adhesions six months prior, presented with chronic abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension over three months. His vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a markedly tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and dullness on percussion. No signs of chronic liver disease were noted. Given his history of small bowel obstruction and the severity of his pain, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The CT scan showed no obstruction or perforation but revealed a large amount of loculated ascites, multiple adhesions with small bowel loops tethered to these adhesions, and hepatomegaly without evidence of cirrhosis or biliary tract obstruction. Laboratory results were as follows: calcium 8.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 650 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 2 g/dL, globulin 5.3 g/dL, aspartate transaminase 20 IU/L, alanine transaminase 33 IU/L, and internationa. Confirmed diagnosis: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis.

Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. His last bowel movement was 2 days ago. On presentation, his vitals were stable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a partial small bowel obstruction. A small bowel follow-through indicated non-specific thickening of the proximal small bowel loops. This was his third hospitalization with the same presentation of small bowel obstruction, with previous admissions one month ago and 2 weeks ago. During the initial hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy showed no findings to suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with push enteroscopy identified enteritis and a Mallory-Weis. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis.

Supine and upright abdominal x-rays should be taken and are usually adequate to diagnose obstruction.

Although only laparotomy can definitively diagnose strangulation, careful serial clinical examination may

provide early warning. Elevated WBCs and acidosis may indicate that strangulation has already occurred.

On plain x-rays, a ladderlike series of distended small-bowel loops is typical of small-bowel obstruction

but may also occur with obstruction of the right colon. Fluid levels in the bowel can be seen in upright

views. Similar, although perhaps less dramatic, x-ray findings and symptoms occur in ileus (paralysis of

the intestine without obstruction—; differentiation can be difficult. Distended loops and fluid

levels may be absent with an obstruction of the upper jejunum or with closed-loop strangulating

obstructions (as may occur with volvulus). Infarcted bowel may produce a mass effect on x-ray. Gas in the

bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis) indicates gangrene.

In large-bowel obstruction, abdominal x-ray shows distention of the colon proximal to the obstruction. In

cecal volvulus, there may be a large gas bubble in the mid-abdomen or left upper quadrant. With both

cecal and sigmoidal volvulus, a contrast enema shows the site of obstruction by a typical "bird-beak"

deformity at the site of the twist; the procedure may actually reduce a sigmoid volvulus. If contrast enema

is not done, colonoscopy can be used to decompress a sigmoid volvulus but rarely works with a cecal

volvulus.

Symptoms and signs include abdominal distention, vomiting, and vague discomfort. Pain rarely has the

classic colicky pattern present in mechanical obstruction. There may be obstipation or passage of slight

amounts of watery stool. Auscultation reveals a silent abdomen or minimal peristalsis. The abdomen is

not tender unless the underlying cause is inflammatory.

Presentation: A 93-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the upper abdomen without signs of peritoneal irritation. His medical history included angina pectoris and previous inguinal hernia surgery, with no record of abdominal surgeries. Laboratory results indicated a white blood cell count of 5.7 × 10^9/l and a C-reactive protein level of 0.15 mmol/l, both within normal ranges.. Confirmed diagnosis: Small bowel volvulus with chylous ascites. Differential diagnosis includes: Small bowel volvulus with chylous ascites.

Presentation: A 22-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a sudden onset of severe abdominal pain that had been progressing for four hours. The pain was described as colicky, diffuse, and non-irradiating. The patient experienced two episodes of vomiting without blood and had a regular bowel movement the previous day. There were no urinary complaints. He had no significant medical history and no prior surgeries. During the physical examination, the patient appeared restless. The abdomen was soft but generally tender upon palpation. Vital signs included a blood pressure of 151/106 mmHg, a pulse rate of 74 beats per minute, and a temperature of 36.0ºC. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 19.3x10^9/L, with all other parameters within normal limits.. Confirmed diagnosis: Chyloperitoneum secondary to primary small-bowel volvulus. Differential diagnosis includes: Chyloperitoneum secondary to primary small-bowel volvulus.

During pregnancy, the hormone progesterone causes smooth muscle to relax, to prevent premature uterine contractions. Progesterone also affects the gut smooth muscle, causing delayed gastric emptying, constipation, and diminished lower esophageal sphincter and anal sphincter tone. Musculoskeletal changes also occur during pregnancy including ligamentous laxity allowing the pelvis to stretch and accommodate the gravid uterus. However, this laxity may ultimately lead to pathology. Additionally, the hormone relaxin, which relaxes the symphysis pubis and cervix during pregnancy, decreases ileal smooth muscle contractions, further contributing to constipation in pregnancy and slowing of small bowel transit.

Lung CT scan has been used to understand the pathophysiology and the interplay with mechanical ventilation. CT scan clearly showed that ARDS is a non-homogeneous lung disease with the following classically reported morphological patterns: consolidated regions (defined by a homogenous increase in density without vessels or bronchi), ground glass areas (with an increase in density with still recognizable vessels) and the normal aerated regions. These three morphological features are usually simultaneously present. Air bronchograms and small pleural effusions are also common. The dependent localization of consolidated areas is related to the increase in lung oedema (i.e. increase in lung weight) during the initial phase of ARDS which raises the hydrostatic pressure transmitted throughout the lung, causing a reduction in lung gas volume and the development of non-aerated lung regions. These poorly or non-aerated lung regions are characterized by a higher inflammation than normally ventilated lung regions. The presence of non-inflated areas causes a major expansion of the neighbouring lung regions and generation of higher local pressures which act as a “stress raiser”. Higher amounts of inhomogeneities are accompanied by higher stress raisers and severity of ARDS and worse outcome. Pulmonary ARDS presents a similar amount of consolidated and ground glass areas while extrapulmonary ARDS has a higher amount of ground glass areas.
