Spasmodic colic is usually characterized in horses by brief intermittent attacks of abdominal pain, pawing, rolling, and kicking the belly for a few minutes, then shaking and standing in a normal way for a few minutes until the next fit of pain reoccurs. Therefore, the affected animal presented with multiple skin wounds (Fig. 3). The horse suffering from spasmodic colic had increased peristaltic activity, which might be attributed to inflammatory conditions such as enteritis and colitis. The ultrasonographic appearance of the abdominal organ showed that the cecum appeared with an echogenic wall, and the contents were of variable echogenicity. The wall thickness increased, and the peristaltic activity of the cecum was hypermotile on real-time ultrasonography. The left ventral colon appeared with increased wall thickness, and sacculations were detected in some cases, whereas, in others, it appeared with normal wall thickness. The descending colon has a thin echogenic wall and contains isoechoic ingesta that appear in continuous motion, indicating hypermotility of the bowel.

Presentation: A 70-year-old male presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and constipation for the past 2 days. He also experienced moderate-to-high-grade fever with chills and rigors. His past and personal history were unremarkable. Physical examination of the abdomen revealed a tender, ill-defined mass in the right iliac fossa. No abnormalities were found on per rectal examination. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia. Abdominal ultrasonography indicated dilated bowel loops without intraperitoneal collection and normal solid organs. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed irregular mural thickening of the cecum and ascending colon up to the hepatic flexure, with an approximate length of 12–13 cm and maximum thickness of 2.7–2.8 cm. Adjacent mesocolonic fat stranding and haziness were observed along with subcentimetric lymph nodes. Distal ileal loops appeared prominent (2.7–2.8 cm in diameter) with a 'small bowel fecal sign'. Colonoscopy was planned for biopsy. After bowel preparation, the patient reported severe abdominal pain and developed generalized tenderness and involuntary guarding. He exhibited tachycardia and appeared toxic. An er. Confirmed diagnosis: Ameboma. Differential diagnosis includes: Ameboma.

Presentation: A 10-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric chronic pain clinic due to persistent pain throughout his body, including headaches, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain, which had been ongoing for several years. The onset of pain began around the age of seven and a half, with no prior medical or surgical history. Over a few weeks, the pain spread to multiple locations including thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, muscular areas, and the head. There were no identified triggering factors. The pain episodes were frequent, almost daily, and lasted from a few seconds to five minutes. The child reported that the pain was sometimes so intense that he could not move or would drop objects. The pain did not disturb his sleep. Cardiological (electrocardiogram) and neurological (standard and prolonged electroencephalogram, brain MRI) assessments showed no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound and a contrast-enhanced abdomen were normal except for slight fecal impaction, which required no specific intervention. Stool analysis and lactose tolerance tests were normal. Pain management included occasional use of ibuprofen, which had limited effectiveness. At the age of 10, due to persistent pain, he wa. Confirmed diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder. Differential diagnosis includes: Autism Spectrum Disorder.

The evaluation of elastase 1 activity in stool is an example of an indirect test. Pancreatic elastase 1 is a very specific human protease (proteolytic enzyme) secreted by pancreatic cells within acini. Elastase 1 is a very stable enzyme, which is not degraded in the alimentary tract, unlike other pancreatic proteases (e.g. chymotrypsin), reflecting pancreatic secretory function; for this reason, it is a good diagnostic test. Indirect testing for faecal elastase 1 applies monoclonal antibody detection (ELISA). This test shows high sensitivity, and its advantages include relatively low cost and non-invasive character. Faecal elastase 1 activity over 200 µg/g is considered normal, reflecting normal pancreatic exocrine function, while the activity within the range of 100–200 µg/g is indicative of a slight pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, and below 100 µg/g suggests severe insufficiency.

Faecal elastase 1 testing has also been implemented in an ongoing Polish study conducted at the Clinical Department of Internal Medicine and Gastroenterology, CSK MSWiA, Warsaw, aiming to evaluate the causes of abdominal symptoms in diabetic patients with a special focus on pancreatic exocrine dysfunction. It is a prospective, cohort, non-randomised study, including 231 patients with type 1 or 2 diabetes. Seventy-seven patients were excluded from the study because of a previous history of pancreatic diseases, alcohol abuse, or smoking. Sixty-seven patients met the inclusion criteria such as the presence of significant abdominal symptoms, while 87 patients from the study group did not present any significant complaints. Further analysis was conducted on 50 patients; 30 of them presenting abdominal symptoms (test group) and 20 without any symptoms (control group). In all patients, HbA1c, faecal elastase 1, lipase, and hydrogen breath test were obtained. In the test group, there was a decrease in elastase 1 concentration below 200 µg/g in 13.33% of diabetic patients, compared to 15% in the control group. In contrast, an increased elastase 1 activity above 60 IU/l was found in 40% in the test group compared to 15% in the control group. Hence, we can assume that changes in lipase and FE-1 in diabetic patients may reflect development of pancreatopathy in the course of diabetes, or so-called diabetic pancreatopathy, or chronic pancreatitis.

Presentation: A 67-year-old male patient reported experiencing belching and abdominal distension for the past year, along with diarrhea for over two months. The patient had no prior history of these symptoms. He had a history of hypertension, which was well managed with medication. There was no personal or family history of related conditions or cancers. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. The patient tested negative for Helicobacter pylori.. Confirmed diagnosis: Serrated Polyposis Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Serrated Polyposis Syndrome.

Presentation: A 2-month-old male (corrected gestational age: 40 weeks) weighing 2 kg was admitted with a 2-month history of abdominal distension. He was born prematurely at 30+2 weeks and developed abdominal distension shortly after birth. One day prior to admission, his condition worsened with persistent vomiting, increased abdominal distension, and cessation of defecation. Abdominal CT revealed distended intestines with multiple air-fluid levels and bowel shadows in the left inguinal region. Chest CT showed double pneumonia with partial consolidation. The patient was diagnosed with abdominal distension, bilateral pneumonia, sepsis, and left inguinal hernia. An exploratory laparotomy was scheduled for the following day. On the day of surgery, the infant presented with significant abdominal distension, tight abdominal wall, and mottled lower extremities. Vital signs included a heart rate of 160 bpm, respiratory rate of 50 bpm, oxygen saturation of 90%, and noninvasive blood pressure of 60/50 mmHg. He had a gastric tube in place for gastrointestinal decompression. Anesthesia was induced with sevoflurane inhalation, gradually increased from 1% to 2.5%, along with intravenous administration of mida. Confirmed diagnosis: Hirschsprung's disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Hirschsprung's disease.

Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is characterized by the inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract and is commonly caused by viral, bacterial, or parasitic pathogens. Deaths from acute diarrheal illness, one of the most common diseases worldwide, are gradually decreasing; however, 440,000 children under the age of 5 years still die annually from this disease, according to the 2018 World Health Organization report. Since the introduction of the rotavirus vaccine, although a reduction in the incidence and mortality of diarrheal illness has been reported, it remains a major disease affecting children. In Korea, examination of the pathogens responsible for acute diarrheal diseases began in 1972, linking the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (KCDC), which was reorganized into the KDCA (Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency), Public Health Center, and Institute of Health and Environment. The monitoring laboratory for acute diarrheal disease (EnterNet-Korea) started operations in 2003. Since 2005, the KCDC has been monitoring pathogens that cause AGE, in patients who visit hospitals with the major symptoms of diarrhea and abdominal pain through a waterborne food disease monitoring network operation project involving 70–192 medical institutions, although the number of organizations participating each year was different. Rotavirus, norovirus, enterovirus, and astrovirus were initially monitored, but sapovirus was added to the watch list in 2009.

The ciguatera poisoning algal-drome typically presents with nonspecific GI, neurological, and cardiovascular complaints. A prodrome of GI symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, typically within 6–12 h of food consumption. This may be followed by symptom resolution or may progress to more serious neurological and cardiovascular illness. Cardiovascular symptoms include bradycardia, heart block, and hemodynamic instability. Neurologic symptoms often appear within 1–2 days following onset of GI symptoms and may include numbness and tingling to extremities, headaches, sensation of loose teeth, nonspecific neuropsychiatric complaints, vertiginous symptoms, and muscle weakness. A sensation of hot and cold reversal, known as “cold allodynia” has also been reported and is described as a burning sensation when touching cold items. This same phenomenon is also seen in some cases of NSP. In severe cases of CP, paresthesias, severe dysesthesia, and hallucinations have been reported. Interestingly, there appears to be regional variability in symptoms likely related to the distinct variation in CTX congener exposures; C-CTX has been known to produce more GI symptoms, whereas P-CTX produces more neurological symptoms, and I-CTX has been documented to produce hallucinations. Post-exposure, there is also a phenomenon of symptom recurrence that has been shown to be triggered by several foods (particularly fish and other meats, nuts, alcohol), weight loss, and exercise. Presentation: A 22-year-old female with a history of depression arrived at the emergency department reporting a week-long experience of epigastric abdominal pain, abdominal distention, constipation, and bloating. She denied having recent fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, sick contacts, or recent travel. Her home medication was fluoxetine. She had no known allergies, asthma, or history of arterial or venous thromboembolism. A review of systems did not indicate any cardiac, neurologic, or renal issues. Physical examination showed moderate abdominal distension and tenderness. An initial abdominopelvic CT scan revealed small intestinal mucosal thickening and a moderate amount of free pelvic fluid. Symptomatic treatment was provided, and she was discharged. Two weeks later, due to worsening abdominal pain and distention, she was readmitted. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis at 18.9 k/µL with peripheral blood eosinophilia at 8.8 k/µL (47%). Liver profile and total protein counts were normal. A repeat CT scan indicated extensive abdominal and pelvic ascites, dilated jejunal loops, mucosal thickening, a few slightly prominent mesenteric lymph nodes, and mild bilateral pleural effusions. No . Confirmed diagnosis: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis. Differential diagnosis includes: Eosinophilic Gastroenteritis.

A physical exam may reveal an increase in abdominal girth and signs of bowel obstruction. Rectal and pelvic examination should be performed in constipated patients. Abdominal distention may be objectively assessed by abdominal inductance plethysmography, an ambulatory device that can continuously measure patients’ abdominal girth. Although there are no validated guidelines for the evaluation of FABD, the Rome IV 2016 working group recommends basic diagnostic tests such as complete blood count (CBC) if anemia is suspected, celiac serology (and if positive, duodenal biopsies should be added), abdominal x-ray to rule out obstruction, and a breath test for the diagnosis of SIBO.

In our study 1/5th of patients had history of previous abdominal surgery. This was higher when compared to studies done in different parts of the country. In contrast it was less when compared with a study done in Nigeria and Turkey. This disparity could be because adhesive intestinal obstruction was the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in the latter studies. In a prospective study done in Greece, all patients with adhesive intestinal obstruction had history of previous abdominal surgery. In contrary to this, our study indicated that 1/3rd of the patients with adhesive intestinal obstruction did not have history of any previous abdominal operation. Some of the identified causes of intestinal adhesions in these patients were intestinal TB, Ovarian Torsion, Meckel's diverticulum and one case related to pregnancy while in the rest the cause remains unknown. Similarly, A study done in Poland implicated that bacterial infections of the peritoneum (e.g., typhoid fever, dysentery, and tuberculosis) to be the cause of adhesive intestinal obstruction in those with no prior abdominal surgery. The most common indication for previous abdominal surgery in our study was Intestinal Obstruction followed by Appendicitis, Abdominal trauma and Pelvic conditions. In contrary, some other literatures showed that the most frequent prior surgical procedure performed was appendectomy. And in a study done in Canada colorectal surgeries and gynecological surgeries accounted for the majority of the previous surgeries done.

Many studies done in our country and also abroad showed that length of hospital stay was highly associated with the management outcome. Similarly, our study showed that patients who stayed for greater than 7 days were about 3 times more likely to have unfavourable outcomes. The other associated factors in our study were previous history of abdominal surgery and previous history of intestinal obstruction which were not seen in other studies. Having previous history of abdominal surgery would increase adhesion/band related comorbities. These patients would also have difficult reoperation as compared to those patients with ‘virgin’ abdomen i.e., those who have not been operated before. This is related to problems related to inadvertent bowel injuries associated with such kinds of abdomens.

Presentation: A 67-year-old Japanese man presented with a 1-day history of nausea, vomiting, and upper abdominal pain. He reported that these symptoms had occurred intermittently for several years and had previously resolved on their own; however, this time they persisted. He had a history of taking medication for hypertension but had no surgical, family, social, or environmental history. Physical examination showed a slightly distended abdomen. Neurological examination was normal. On admission, his vital signs were: blood pressure 152/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 beats per minute, and body temperature 36.5 °C. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 11,900 cells/μL with 82.6% segmented neutrophils. Abdominal radiography showed a significantly dilated small intestine with some air-fluid levels.. Confirmed diagnosis: Small intestine volvulus caused by mesenteric lipoma. Presentation: A 19-year-old female arrived at the emergency department with complaints of epigastric abdominal pain and nausea, without additional symptoms. Diagnosing SUI based on classic symptoms can be easily confirmed during pelvic examination, by asking the patient to cough or Valsalva with a full bladder. If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Urodynamic testing can also be performed to confirm a suspected diagnosis of SUI, however, based on the Value of Urodynamic Evaluation study, in women with uncomplicated SUI without significant prolapse or urinary urgency, if SUI is demonstrated on examination, additional urodynamic testing is not necessary before treatment. UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 20-year-old male patient presented with a 10-year history of right-sided ear discharge. The discharge was mucopurulent, scant to moderate in amount, continuous, foul-smelling, occasionally blood-tinged, and associated with hearing loss. There was no history of topical ear drops reaching the throat. Otoendoscopy revealed erosion of the scutum, adherence of the pars tensa over the promontory, and absence of visible ossicles. The tympanic segment of the fallopian canal was visible with the drum draped over it, and a small perforation was noted in the antero-superior quadrant near the opening of the Eustachian tube. No clinical findings indicated complications such as facial palsy, dizziness, tinnitus, or cranial neuropathy. The opposite ear was normal. The Rinne’s test was negative for all three frequencies (256, 512, 1,024 Hz) on the right side and negative for 256 Hz only on the left side. The Weber’s test with 512 Hz was lateralized to the left side. A pure tone audiogram showed profound mixed hearing loss on the right side (100 dB HL) and mild conductive hearing loss on the left side (31 dB HL).. Confirmed diagnosis: Impacted Incus Foreign Body in the Eustachian Tube. Differential diagnosis includes: Impacted Incus Foreign Body in the Eustachian Tube.

Differential diagnosis includes: Actinomycosis of the middle turbinate.

Patients without signs or symptoms should be monitored for food avoidance and fluid intake. The monitoring period is very important for the further management of the patients. In summary, unknown primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma accounts for less than 5% of all head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. The diagnostic work-up is highly variable among different institutions and despite a thorough diagnostic work-up, many patients with a metastatic lymph node to the neck end up with an unidentified primary tumor. Upon initial evaluation of a patient with an unknown primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a good clinical history should be obtained, addressing the patient’s symptoms and risk factors; a thorough physical examination, looking and feeling for oral cavity, oropharynx and head and neck skin abnormalities, in addition to the flexible endoscopy exam in office, complemented by narrow band imaging (if available) are recommended. Following history and physical examination (Fig. 1), diagnostic imaging with a contrast-enhanced neck CT and a fusion FDG-PET/CT covering at least the areas from the mid-skull to the thigh can aid on the identification of not only the primary tumor site, but other regional and distant disease sites, which will affect treatment recommendations. A contrast-enhanced neck MRI should be considered in those who have contra-indications for the iodine contrast used on CT imaging, or for those whose CT images are affected by dental artifacts. Directed biopsy of the abnormal clinical or imaging findings is recommended for histologic confirmation. Presentation: A 53-year-old male reported experiencing horizontal double vision and eye pain for the past 2 months. His medical history indicated a neck mass persisting for 10 months, along with a runny nose and nasal blockage for 3 months. Additional symptoms included right-sided headache, eye pain, right nasal blockage, and tinnitus. The patient has a smoking history of approximately 20 pack-years but no significant weight loss or head injury. Ophthalmic examination revealed a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Both anterior and posterior segment examinations were normal in both eyes. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and pupil sizes were equal bilaterally. Orthoptic examination showed left esotropia of 45 prism diopters (PD) at distance and 50 PD at near, with worsening esotropia in left gaze. Ocular motility was normal in the right eye, but a significant abduction deficit was noted in the left eye, preventing movement across the midline. Sensory examination of cranial nerve areas V1-V3 was normal.. Confirmed diagnosis: non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

As clinical localization of symptoms to the brachial plexus is difficult, ultrasound is a good means of screening for brachial plexus pathology. A negative ultrasound examination effectively excludes most brachial plexus pathology. The likelihood of finding an abnormality on MRI when ultrasound examination is negative is extremely low. Ultrasound is as accurate as MRI in the detection of brachial plexus pathology. Ultrasound can be performed relatively quickly compared to MRI and allows ready comparison of both sides. Also, high-quality ultrasound of the brachial plexus is not usually affected by body habitus like other body areas, such as abdominal ultrasound. Standard ultrasound of the brachial plexus, which involves examination of both sides, can be completed in 15 min. The cost is similar to other neck ultrasound examinations. Ultrasound for suspected thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) can take 45 min to complete.

Presentation: A 65-year-old male reported experiencing positional vertigo for 17 years, typically triggered by rolling in bed to either side, occasionally accompanied by mild headaches. He did not report any visual disturbances, nausea, vomiting, temporary vision loss, double vision, speech difficulties, sensitivity to light and sound, or ear-related symptoms such as tinnitus, ear tightness, or hearing loss. The vertigo episodes lasted for more than 10 seconds. His medical history was unremarkable. During the examination, no spontaneous nystagmus was observed. Visual eye movement, video head impulse testing, and the Romberg test results were normal. However, left-beating nystagmus was noted during the left Dix-Hallpike test and the left roll test, persisting for over one minute.. Confirmed diagnosis: Choroid Plexus Tumor. Differential diagnosis includes: Choroid Plexus Tumor.

Presentation: A 1-year-old male child presented with a history of an enlarged head and irritability over the past 3 months, along with occasional vomiting. There was no history of fever, visual disturbances, speech issues, or involvement of cranial nerves. The child did not experience altered consciousness, seizures, head trauma, or contact with tuberculosis. Physical examination was normal. Neurological examination showed the child was conscious. Fundoscopy indicated bilateral papilledema, and vision was generally normal. No other cranial nerve involvement was noted. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Skull radiographs showed sutural separation with a silver-beaten appearance. MRI of the brain revealed a large mass in the posterior horn of the right lateral ventricle attached by a pedicle, accompanied by moderate hydrocephalus.. Confirmed diagnosis: Choroid Plexus Papilloma. Differential diagnosis includes: Choroid Plexus Papilloma.

The examination should include anthropometric measurements and a detailed clinical assessment of critical systems (skin, ears, nose, mouth, throat, and chest). General assessment is even more important in children with a history of long-term corticosteroid use to highlight the presence of drug-induced adverse effects. Typical abnormalities include Dennie-Morgan lines, the allergic salute, allergic shiners, and mouth breathing. All these clinical points are collectively characterized as the ‘allergic facies.’ Nasal examination provides significant information and can be performed through anterior rhinoscopy using a common otoscope. Often, this can reveal secretions (clear and watery in cases of allergic rhinitis, dense and discolored in cases of non-allergic or infectious rhinitis), polyps, foreign bodies, nasal septal deviation, nasal septal perforation, nasal creases, and nasal mucosal swelling. Endoscopic examination of the nose using a specialized endoscope is not obligatory during the investigation. However, it can be helpful when the child’s symptoms persist throughout the year to rule out anatomical anomalies or non-allergic inflammatory conditions (e.g., chronic rhinosinusitis with/without nasal polyps). Endoscopy is also valuable for assessing the patency of the nasal cavities, the size of adenoids, and the presence of nasal lesions. From a functional perspective, it is crucial to evaluate the airflow from the nasal cavities (nasal ventilation) to detect unilateral or bilateral obstruction.

RP evolves through inflammatory flares and remission phases, with the risk of developing severe manifestations such as respiratory manifestations. Myelodysplastic syndrome was considered a poor prognosis marker prior to the discovery of VEXAS syndrome, explaining the specific phenotype described in previous studies. Besides myelodysplastic syndrome, respiratory and cardiac involvement remain the most severe disease manifestations that affect the prognosis. The study conducted by Dion et al.  found an overall survival probability of 94% and 83% at 5 years and 10 years, respectively, from the first symptoms but the respiratory manifestation cluster shows a decrease in survival later, after 20–30 years of follow-up. Recently, Shimizu et al.  compared cohorts of RP patients in 2009 and 2019. Mortality decreased significantly over the decade, from 9% in 2009 to 2% in 2019, which could be related to a decrease in the prevalence of airway involvement (49% in 2009, 37% in 2019). The improvement in survival can be explained by the expansion of therapeutic options, with immunosuppressive therapies and biotherapies, that allow rapid and prolonged control of the disease, as soon as the diagnosis is made with less side effects due to steroid treatments. Activity [Relapsing Polychondritis Disease Activity Index ] and damages [Relapsing Polychondritis Damage Index ] scores have been developed to facilitate the follow-up of RP patients and the assessment of treatment response. Presentation: A 74-year-old male with a history of a condition diagnosed in 2015, currently on maintenance chemotherapy, underwent a follow-up FDG PET/CT in August 2022. This imaging showed nonavid bilateral maxillary sinus disease, which was interpreted as benign. In September 2022, he presented with symptoms including bilateral nasal congestion (more severe on the right side), obstructed nasal flow, facial pain and pressure, discolored drainage, and a foul taste and odor. These symptoms had been present since January 2022, following a COVID-19 diagnosis. Initial symptom relief was achieved with nightly use of Afrin and Xylitol, but symptoms became refractory. Despite seeing an ENT provider and undergoing a course of antibiotics and prednisone, there was no improvement. He was referred to our institution's ENT department in September. An endoscopic endonasal examination identified bilateral nasal masses with pulsatile and vascular characteristics. Further evaluation with sinus CT and contrast-enhanced brain and orbit MRI revealed progressive osseous erosion and dehiscence of the maxillary sinuses, along with bilateral enhancing masses showing trans-osseous extension.. Confirmed diagnosis: Extramedullary Plasmacytoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Extramedullary Plasmacytoma.

Presentation: An 11-year-old male presented with bilateral nasal bleeding occurring four times over the past day, described as massive by the family. The patient also exhibited a skin rash that appeared a day before the nasal bleeding began. Additionally, there was a history of loss of appetite and significant, though unquantified, weight loss over the past month. There was no history of fever, cough, bleeding disorders, connective tissue disorders, autoimmune disorders, or cancer in the patient or his family. Upon examination, all vital signs were normal. A dry clot was observed in both nostrils, and there were no signs of anemia. Chest examination revealed scattered inspiratory crackles in the upper lung zones bilaterally. No organomegaly was detected. A petechial rash was noted on the chest, back, and upper extremities.. Confirmed diagnosis: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura. Differential diagnosis includes: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura.

Presentation: A 48-year-old female presented with bilateral breast pain and palpable masses. Mammography (MMG) identified multiple well-circumscribed, equal density masses in the upper outer quadrants of both breasts. Ultrasonography (US) detected multiple anechoic or complex solid and cystic masses in the same regions. Several masses in the upper quadrant of the left breast appeared as anechoic and complex solid masses and cystic masses without vascularity on Doppler ultrasound. The patient did not disclose her mammoplasty history during the examination.. Confirmed diagnosis: Foreign body reaction due to polyacrylamide gel mammoplasty. Differential diagnosis includes: Foreign body reaction due to polyacrylamide gel mammoplasty.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed. The initial suspected diagnosis, made with insufficient features and no spirometry testing, gradually, and with no evidence, becomes a definitive diagnosis rarely questioned in the fut

Asthma diagnosis is often suspected when a constellation of typical features is present, however, as most guidelines highlight, diagnosis has to be confirmed either by objective tests or an objective response to treatment. One of the initial major error that occurs is that insufficient features of the asthma pattern are sought before the diagnosis is made. Patient's history should always give enough answers to the following question: “Does the child have any or all of cough, wheeze and breathlessness?.” A persistent cough (especially if non-productive) alone in an otherwise well-child is highly unlikely be due to asthma. The medical term wheezing is often used by parents to describe different sounds and care should be taken to be sure what they actually mean. The habit to ask the family to try to demonstrate the sound of wheezing yourself, could help to avoid misunderstanding. It is also important to understand if the child is noisy and breathless at the same time and to assess the severity of symptoms. After an intense exercise, breathlessness is common but a formal diagnosis of asthma or exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction (EILO) is correct only in about half of those complaining of symptoms. The rest of adolescents are just deconditioned or exaggerating their symptoms. The possibility of fabricated and induced illness should be also excluded and possible personal or family psychological factors should be investigated. While random biopsies have traditionally been performed, they are no longer recommended with the advent of modern imaging due to low diagnostic yield. However, in the event that examination under anesthesia with directed biopsies fail to yield positive results, ipsilateral tonsillectomy, and base of tongue mucosectomy (or lingual tonsillectomy) are recommended. In a study of 236 patients, the tonsillar fossa and base of tongue were identified as the most common primary sites of unknown primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with a rate of 44.7% and 43.9%, respectively. In patients whose primary tumor site has not been identified on clinical exam and imaging studies, Cianchetti et al demonstrated that examination under anesthesia with directed biopsy and/or ipsilateral tonsillectomy identified the primary tumor site in 44.3% of patients. In addition, Waltonen et al found that ipsilateral tonsillectomy was superior to deep tonsillar biopsy (29.6% vs. 3.2%, P = .0002) in its ability to detect the occult primary site. Similarly, Tanzler et al showed that within the palatine tonsils, a radical ipsilateral tonsillectomy improves the chances of identifying an occult tumor (39%) than biopsy alone (13%). While the merits of ipsilateral versus bilateral tonsillectomy have been widely debated, recent studies are in favor of bilateral tonsillectomy, as there seems to be a small risk of an occult malignancy in the contralateral tonsil, and the morbidity associated with the procedure is not significantly increased.

Anosmia is complete loss of smell. Hyposmia is partial loss of smell. Most patients with anosmia have

normal perception of salty, sweet, sour, and bitter substances but lack flavor discrimination, which largely

depends on olfaction. Therefore, they often complain of losing the sense of taste (ageusia) and of not

enjoying food. If unilateral, anosmia is often unrecognized.

Presentation: A 41-year-old male visited the ENT clinic in Pisa in November 2018, reporting bilateral nasal blockage, nasal discharge, and snoring. The patient had no history of smoking, allergies, or asthma but had a family history of autoimmune conditions. Examination using flexible fiberoptic endoscopy of the nasal cavity showed enlarged inferior turbinates on both sides and a deviated nasal septum with a noticeable left ridge. Additionally, a nonspecific lesion was observed on the posterior wall near the right torus tubarius in the nasopharynx. The lesion appeared inflammatory and resembled adenoid hypertrophy with postnasal drip secretions.. Confirmed diagnosis: nasopharyngeal sarcoidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: nasopharyngeal sarcoidosis.

Presentation: A 12-year-old boy was referred from a local private clinic due to swelling on the right side of his face. The child reported right-sided nasal obstruction, episodes of epistaxis, and watery nasal discharge for two months, along with a mass in the right nasal cavity. The epistaxis episodes were painless, lasting 15 to 20 minutes each, with blood loss of 30 to 40 ml. The patient exhibited clear mouth breathing, particularly during sleep, and did not report any headaches. There was no history of similar epistaxis episodes prior to two months ago. Extraoral examination revealed significant facial asymmetry caused by swelling over the right cheek. The swelling extended from the infraorbital margin superiorly to the lower border of the mandible inferiorly, and from the ala of the nose and corner of the mouth anteriorly to the tragus of the ear and ramus of the mandible posteriorly. The swelling measured 7 cm × 6 cm, had smooth, well-defined margins, and was firm in consistency. It was tender, compressible, and pulsatile upon palpation. Intraoral examination was normal. The patient showed no signs of pallor, and routine hematological tests were within normal limits. Diagnostic nasal endos. Confirmed diagnosis: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma. Differential diagnosis includes: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma.

Presentation: A 57-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypothyroidism, and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted to the hospital presenting with cough, progressive shortness of breath, low-grade fever, joint pain, ear discharge from both ears with hearing loss in the left ear, bloody nasal discharge, nasal obstruction with severe crusting, and peripheral left facial nerve paralysis. Physical examination showed bloody nasal discharge, nasal crusting, hearing loss, left facial nerve paralysis, dyspnea, cough, and wheezing on auscultation, with a pulse oxygen saturation of 89%. Laboratory tests indicated leukocytosis (14.4 G/l), thrombocytosis (PLT 606 G/l), significantly elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein – CRP: 100 mg/l, erythrocyte sedimentation rate – ESR: 90 mm/h), proteinuria, and an active urine sediment containing red and white cells. Plasma creatinine levels were normal. Immunological tests revealed the presence of cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA 1:40, n < 1:10 U/ml) and anti-proteinase 3 antibodies (anti-PR3 27 U/ml, n < 20 U/ml). Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative. A nasal swab culture show. Confirmed diagnosis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.

NDs may present as a cyst, sinus, or fistula located anywhere from the philtrum of the upper lip to the glabellar region. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Owusu-Aim et al. revealed that 50% of children have at least one local infection by the age of 4, and more than 90% before their 9th birthday. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Prodromal symptoms, such as fever and headache, were mild, and local rash at the site of contact was the initial symptom in some reported cases. Other symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, nasal discharge, oral ulcers, sore throat, weight loss, abdominal pain, and diarrhea were reported too. Mucosal lesions, however, can be extremely painful and in severe cases might result in the perforation of the rectal wall.

Presentation: A 64-year-old Saudi female from the Eastern Province presented with several months of progressive nasal obstruction on one side and recurrent episodes of nosebleeds. She did not report any loss of smell, nasal discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing, facial pain, or headache. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes, with no significant family medical history. A rigid endoscopic examination revealed a large polypoidal mass on the left side of the nasal cavity with smooth mucosa, completely blocking the left nasal passage. Other examinations of the ear, nose, throat, head, and neck were normal, and there were no palpable lymph nodes. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses with contrast showed a lobulated mass on the left anterior side at the level of the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum, with mild heterogeneous enhancement after IV contrast and bone remodeling. There was no extension into the paranasal sinuses or apparent bone invasion.. Confirmed diagnosis: Nasal Septal Schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Nasal Septal Schwannoma.

Presentation: A 31-year-old male of Eastern European origin presented with a 3-month history of unilateral nasal obstruction, swelling, and sporadic, short-lasting episodes of epistaxis. He reported swelling of the right lateral nasal wall. Examination revealed a large, right-sided nasal polypoidal mass occluding most of the right nasal airway. The mucosa appeared smooth and healthy, but the nasal septum was significantly deviated to the left. Endoscopic examination of the pharynx, larynx, and contralateral side of the nose was normal. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the rest of the ear, nose, and throat, as well as physical examinations, were normal. Non-contrast CT of the sinonasal region showed a soft tissue lesion arising from the right side of the nasal septum. MRI imaging of the lesion indicated a general increased T2 signal with heterogeneous nodular T2 heterogeneity. The unenhanced axial T1-weighted sequence revealed a small focus of T1 shortening, consistent with low volume focal cystic degeneration within the tumor.. Confirmed diagnosis: nasal septal schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: nasal septal schwannoma.

Presentation: A 40-year-old male presented with a 10-month history of watery nasal discharge. He also reported a history of headaches and nasal obstruction, previously attributed to hypertrophied turbinate, for which surgery was recommended but declined. Over the past 2 years, the patient experienced a gradual onset of anosmia, initially without watery discharge but associated with nasal obstruction. The watery nasal discharge increased when bending forward or coughing and trickled into the nasopharynx without any detectable taste. This discharge was also associated with headaches. The patient has no history of nasal trauma, surgery, or signs of meningitis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele. Differential diagnosis includes: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele.

Presentation: A 50-year-old woman presented on March 27, 2016, with complaints of bloody phlegm and a sensation of a foreign body in the pharynx for 3 years. She had no history of hoarseness, chest tightness, dyspnea, dysphagia, nasal obstruction, headache, dizziness, or tinnitus. Previously, she was treated with antibiotics for gingival bleeding and pharyngitis at a local hospital without improvement. At our hospital, laryngoscopy revealed a red, peanut-sized neoplasm with a smooth surface, soft texture, and a tendency to bleed on the free margin of the caudal nasal septum. The nasopharyngeal mucosa on both sides was smooth. The patient was admitted for surgery. Physical examination showed no enlarged lymph nodes in the head and neck regions. Axial computed tomography (CT) showed a round, soft tissue shadow on the caudal nasal septum. Preoperative tests showed no contraindications for surgery. Endoscopic resection of the nasopharyngeal mass was performed under general anesthesia. During the procedure, the bilateral nasal mucosa was contracted, and no obstruction was found in the bilateral nasal cavity. A red neoplasm with a smooth surface and a tendency to bleed was observed in the caudal nasal. Confirmed diagnosis: Thyroid-like low-grade nasopharyngeal papillary adenocarcinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Thyroid-like low-grade nasopharyngeal papillary adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis is suspected clinically. Other disorders to consider include trauma, insect or animal bites

without cellulitis, retained foreign bodies, allergic reactions, tumors, and inflammatory orbital

pseudotumor.

Eyelid swelling may require the use of lid retractors for evaluation of the globe, and initial signs of

complicated infection may be subtle. An ophthalmologist should be consulted when orbital cellulitis is

suspected.

Preseptal cellulitis and orbital cellulitis are often distinguishable clinically. Preseptal cellulitis is likely if eye

findings are normal except for eyelid swelling. The presence of a local nidus of infection on the skin

makes preseptal cellulitis even more likely.

If findings are equivocal, if the examination is difficult (as in young children), or if nasal discharge is

present (suggesting sinusitis), CT or MRI should be done to confirm orbital cellulitis, to exclude tumor and

pseudotumor, and to diagnose sinusitis if present. MRI is better than CT if cavernous sinus thrombosis is

being considered.

The direction of proptosis may be a clue to the site of infection; eg, extension from the frontal sinus

pushes the globe down and out, and extension from the ethmoid sinus pushes the globe laterally and out.

Blood cultures are often done (ideally before beginning antibiotics) in patients with orbital cellulitis but are

positive in less than one third. Lumbar puncture is done if meningitis is suspected. Cultures of the

paranasal sinus fluid are done if sinusitis is the suspected source. Other laboratory tests are not

particularly helpful

Vital signs are reviewed, particularly for presence of fever.

The nose is examined for discharge and foreign body.

The mouth is examined for signs of gum disease, dental infection, and cancer. Signs of apparent dryness

are noted (eg, whether the mucosa is dry, sticky, or moist; whether saliva is foamy, stringy, or normal in

appearance).

The pharynx is examined for signs of infection and cancer.

Sniff test:

A sniff test of exhaled air is conducted. In general, oral causes result in a putrefying, pungent

smell, whereas systemic conditions result in a more subtle, abnormal odor. Ideally, for 48 h before the

examination, the patient avoids eating garlic or onions, and for 2 h before, the patient abstains from

eating,

chewing, drinking, gargling, rinsing, or smoking. During the test, the patient exhales 10 cm away

from the examiner's nose, first through the mouth and then with the mouth closed. A worse odor through

the mouth suggests an oral etiology. A worse odor through the nose suggests a nasal or sinus etiology.

Similar odor through both nose and mouth suggests a systemic or pulmonary cause. If site of origin is

unclear, the posterior tongue is scraped with a plastic spoon. After 5 sec, the spoon is sniffed 5 cm from

the examiner's nose.

Presentation: A 45-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with a history of bloody nasal discharge, hemoptysis, and rash for 11 years, which worsened over the past 2 weeks. Additionally, he experienced abdominal pain and melena for the past month. The patient also presented with rashes on his face, trunk, limbs, and feet, as well as oral ulcers, perianal ulcers, and sinusitis. Leucocytes count of 8.5 × 109/L, hemoglobin level of 79 g/L, urine protein (+), microhematuria (+), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h, c-ANCA with a titre of 1 in 100, and PR3-ANCA of > 200 RU/ml. CT revealed left frontal and ethmoid sinusitis, and bilateral maxillary sinusitis. Colonic biopsies revealed inflammatory granulation tissues. The membrane biopsy revealed degenerative colonic mucosal tissues, while the colonic biopsy revealed inflammatory granulation tissues without normal colon glands.. Confirmed diagnosis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.

Presentation: A 9-year-old boy presented with low-grade fever, chest pain, breathlessness, and thick yellow nasal discharge. He had a history of treatment for allergic sinusitis and bronchial asthma since the age of 3. At 4 years old, he was treated with anti-tuberculosis therapy due to small opacities in the lung observed radiologically, despite being sputum negative. He also reported expectoration with brown-colored sputum. Over the years, he received multiple treatments including antibiotics, antihistamines, corticosteroids (both nasal and inhaled), and bronchodilators, but his symptoms persisted. Confirmed diagnosis: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis with Aspergillus Sinusitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis with Aspergillus Sinusitis.

Presentation: An 11-year-old girl presented with nasal blockage, recurrent nasal discharge, and open mouth breathing for 3 years. Recently, her parents observed an abnormal swelling inside her mouth, which developed gradually, was painless, and progressively increased in size. There were no additional complaints related to the ears or throat. Physical examination identified a smooth, pinkish mass hanging in the oropharynx, located posterior to the left palatine tonsil. Flexible nasal endoscopy revealed a pedunculated mass originating from the left lateral wall of the nasopharynx, just posterior to the Eustachian tube. The remainder of the clinical examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography (CT) showed a well-circumscribed, heterogeneous mass without intracranial extension, originating from the nasopharynx.. Presentation: A 53-year-old male reported experiencing horizontal double vision and eye pain for the past 2 months. His medical history indicated a neck mass persisting for 10 months, along with a runny nose and nasal blockage for 3 months. Additional symptoms included right-sided headache, eye pain, right nasal blockage, and tinnitus. The patient has a smoking history of approximately 20 pack-years but no significant weight loss or head injury. Ophthalmic examination revealed a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Both anterior and posterior segment examinations were normal in both eyes. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and pupil sizes were equal bilaterally. Orthoptic examination showed left esotropia of 45 prism diopters (PD) at distance and 50 PD at near, with worsening esotropia in left gaze. Ocular motility was normal in the right eye, but a significant abduction deficit was noted in the left eye, preventing movement across the midline. Sensory examination of cranial nerve areas V1-V3 was normal.. Confirmed diagnosis: non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Presentation: A 57-year-old male reported experiencing horizontal binocular double vision for 5 months, followed by the discovery of a lump on the left side of his neck, nosebleeds, and ringing in the ears. He did not experience headaches, eye pain, nasal blockage, or reduced sense of smell. There was no significant weight loss or brain injury during this period. He had no systemic diseases and no history of smoking. An eye examination showed a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/25 in both eyes. The anterior and posterior segments of the eyes were normal. Pupillary responses were normal with no relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and pupil sizes were equal in both eyes. An orthoptic examination revealed right esotropia of 30 prism diopters (PD) at distance and 40 PD at near, with worsening in right gaze. Eye movement was normal in the left eye, but the right eye showed significantly limited abduction, unable to cross the midline. Sensation in the areas served by cranial nerves V1-V3 was intact. Two weeks later, the patient reported significantly blurred vision in the right eye. An eye examination showed a BCVA of hand motion in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, with grade II. Confirmed diagnosis: Non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Facial trauma resulting in epistaxis may indicate a nasal fracture. Other symptoms and signs include

obvious or subtle nasal deformity, swelling, point tenderness, crepitus, and instability. Lacerations,

ecchymosis (nasal and periorbital), septal deviation, and nasal obstruction may be present. Septal

hematoma appears as a purplish bulge on the septum. CSF rhinorrhea appears as clear drainage but

may be mixed with blood, making it difficult to identify.

Diagnosis is based on physical examination. Plain x-rays of an uncomplicated nasal fracture are not

helpful because their sensitivity and specificity are poor. If other facial fractures or complications are

suspected, CT of facial bones is done.

Presentation: A 12-year-old boy was referred from a local private clinic due to swelling on the right side of his face. The child reported right-sided nasal obstruction, episodes of epistaxis, and watery nasal discharge for two months, along with a mass in the right nasal cavity. The epistaxis episodes were painless, lasting 15 to 20 minutes each, with blood loss of 30 to 40 ml. The patient exhibited clear mouth breathing, particularly during sleep, and did not report any headaches. There was no history of similar epistaxis episodes prior to two months ago. Extraoral examination revealed significant facial asymmetry caused by swelling over the right cheek. The swelling extended from the infraorbital margin superiorly to the lower border of the mandible inferiorly, and from the ala of the nose and corner of the mouth anteriorly to the tragus of the ear and ramus of the mandible posteriorly. The swelling measured 7 cm × 6 cm, had smooth, well-defined margins, and was firm in consistency. It was tender, compressible, and pulsatile upon palpation. Intraoral examination was normal. The patient showed no signs of pallor, and routine hematological tests were within normal limits. Diagnostic nasal endos. Confirmed diagnosis: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma. Differential diagnosis includes: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma.

NDs may present as a cyst, sinus, or fistula located anywhere from the philtrum of the upper lip to the glabellar region. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Owusu-Aim et al. revealed that 50% of children have at least one local infection by the age of 4, and more than 90% before their 9th birthday. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Intracranial involvement is estimated in 20% of cases but ranges from 4% to 57% in different studies, and it is impossible to determine clinically as there is no correlation between the location of the sinus ostium or cyst and the presence of a

The diagnostic protocol is similar for NDs, NGHs, and EPHCs. Computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remain the standards for presurgical management in all midface nasal masses. Regarding NDs, MRI presents slightly higher values of sensitivity, specificity, predictive positive value, and predictive negative value towards intracranial extension in NDs compared to CT. Therefore, MRI plays a pivotal role in diagnostics and should be the first-choice radiological tool. Many researchers agree; nevertheless, the complimentary role of CT should be highlighted. Both false-positive and false-negative results are still reported despite advances in radiological imaging. Even regarding solely NDs, numerous needless craniotomies resulting from false-positive imaging findings have been reported. The most frequent radiological pitfalls have been described in previous publications. These usually stem from uncompleted endochondral ossification processes of anterior cranial fossa.

Presentation: A 64-year-old Saudi female from the Eastern Province presented with several months of progressive nasal obstruction on one side and recurrent episodes of nosebleeds. She did not report any loss of smell, nasal discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing, facial pain, or headache. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes, with no significant family medical history. A rigid endoscopic examination revealed a large polypoidal mass on the left side of the nasal cavity with smooth mucosa, completely blocking the left nasal passage. Other examinations of the ear, nose, throat, head, and neck were normal, and there were no palpable lymph nodes. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses with contrast showed a lobulated mass on the left anterior side at the level of the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum, with mild heterogeneous enhancement after IV contrast and bone remodeling. There was no extension into the paranasal sinuses or apparent bone invasion.. Confirmed diagnosis: Nasal Septal Schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Nasal Septal Schwannoma.

Interpretation of findings:

Sudden onset after significant head trauma or toxin exposure strongly

implicates that event as the cause.

A history of chronic rhinosinusitis is suggestive, particularly when significant congestion, polyps, or both

are visible on examination. However, because these findings are common in the population, the physician

should be wary of missing another disorder. Progressive confusion and recent memory loss in an elderly

patient suggest Alzheimer's disease as a cause. Waxing and waning neurologic symptoms affecting

multiple areas suggest a neurodegenerative disease such as multiple sclerosis. Slowly progressive

anosmia in an elderly patient with no other symptoms or findings suggests normal aging as the cause.

Presentation: A 31-year-old male of Eastern European origin presented with a 3-month history of unilateral nasal obstruction, swelling, and sporadic, short-lasting episodes of epistaxis. He reported swelling of the right lateral nasal wall. Examination revealed a large, right-sided nasal polypoidal mass occluding most of the right nasal airway. The mucosa appeared smooth and healthy, but the nasal septum was significantly deviated to the left. Endoscopic examination of the pharynx, larynx, and contralateral side of the nose was normal. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the rest of the ear, nose, and throat, as well as physical examinations, were normal. Non-contrast CT of the sinonasal region showed a soft tissue lesion arising from the right side of the nasal septum. MRI imaging of the lesion indicated a general increased T2 signal with heterogeneous nodular T2 heterogeneity. The unenhanced axial T1-weighted sequence revealed a small focus of T1 shortening, consistent with low volume focal cystic degeneration within the tumor.. Confirmed diagnosis: nasal septal schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: nasal septal schwannoma.

Presentation: A 70-year-old male reported experiencing mild pain, watering, and discharges from his left eye, along with restricted eye movement for six months. His medical history was unremarkable except for participation in a community bath. Upon examination, his vision was measured at 20/40, and he had a senile cataract. The globe was intact, with mild ptosis and restricted eye movement in all lateral directions. Intra-ocular pressure (IOP) was normal, and there was regurgitation of pressure over the lacrimal sac. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the left orbit in axial and coronal planes depicted a predominantly intraconal soft tissue density mass lesion measuring 2.5 (AP) × 1.5 (ML) × 1.5 (CC) cm3 involving the medial rectus and posterior aspect of the superior rectus muscle. MRI revealed a well-defined T2 hypointense lesion in the left orbit involving the medial rectus and extending to the postero-medial aspect of the superior rectus, abutting the lateral part of the left optic nerve sheath. It was heterogeneously enhanced with contrast.. Confirmed diagnosis: Intra-Orbital Wooden Foreign Body. Differential diagnosis includes: Intra-Orbital Wooden Foreign Body.

Imaging findings in a 72-year-old male patient presenting with strabismus and diplopia diagnosed with sinonasal mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Computed tomography images (a) reveal sclerosis and a lytic destructive appearance extending to the clivus in the sphenoid bone (black arrows). Magnetic resonance imaging reveals the lesion as iso-hypointense on T1-weighted (T1W) (b) and slightly hyperintense signal on T2-weighted (c) sequences (white arrows). Post-contrast T1W axial (d) and sagittal (e) images demonstrate invasion from the sphenoid sinus to the sphenoid wing, nasal cavity, cavernous sinuses, and skull base (short arrows). The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map (f) reveals hypointensity and low ADC values (arrowheads). Histopathological examination confirmed high-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. The patient is undergoing concurrent chemoradiotherapy after surgery.

excerpts.finding_text: New symptoms: nasal discharge with worsening pain
excerpts.text: Presentation: A 12-year-old boy was referred from a local private clinic due to swelling on the right side of his face. The child reported right-sided nasal obstruction, episodes of epistaxis, and watery nasal discharge for two months, along with a mass in the right nasal cavity. The epistaxis episodes were painless, lasting 15 to 20 minutes each, with blood loss of 30 to 40 ml. The patient exhibited clear mouth breathing, particularly during sleep, and did not report any headaches. There was no history of similar epistaxis episodes prior to two months ago. Extraoral examination revealed significant facial asymmetry caused by swelling over the right cheek. The swelling extended from the infraorbital margin superiorly to the lower border of the mandible inferiorly, and from the ala of the nose and corner of the mouth anteriorly to the tragus of the ear and ramus of the mandible posteriorly. The swelling measured 7 cm × 6 cm, had smooth, well-defined margins, and was firm in consistency. It was tender, compressible, and pulsatile upon palpation. Intraoral examination was normal. The patient showed no signs of pallor, and routine hematological tests were within normal limits. Diagnostic nasal endos. Confirmed diagnosis: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma. Differential diagnosis includes: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma.

excerpts.text: NDs may present as a cyst, sinus, or fistula located anywhere from the philtrum of the upper lip to the glabellar region. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Owusu-Aim et al. revealed that 50% of children have at least one local infection by the age of 4, and more than 90% before their 9th birthday. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. excerpts.text: The diagnostic protocol is similar for NDs, NGHs, and EPHCs. Computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remain the standards for presurgical management in all midface nasal masses. Regarding NDs, MRI presents slightly higher values of sensitivity, specificity, predictive positive value, and predictive negative value towards intracranial extension in NDs compared to CT. Therefore, MRI plays a pivotal role in diagnostics and should be the first-choice radiological tool. Many researchers agree; nevertheless, the complimentary role of CT should be highlighted. Both false-positive and false-negative results are still reported despite advances in radiological imaging. Even regarding solely NDs, numerous needless craniotomies resulting from false-positive imaging findings have been reported. The most frequent radiological pitfalls have been described in previous publications. These usually stem from uncompleted endochondral ossification processes of anterior cranial fossa.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 64-year-old Saudi female from the Eastern Province presented with several months of progressive nasal obstruction on one side and recurrent episodes of nosebleeds. She did not report any loss of smell, nasal discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing, facial pain, or headache. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes, with no significant family medical history. A rigid endoscopic examination revealed a large polypoidal mass on the left side of the nasal cavity with smooth mucosa, completely blocking the left nasal passage. Other examinations of the ear, nose, throat, head, and neck were normal, and there were no palpable lymph nodes. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses with contrast showed a lobulated mass on the left anterior side at the level of the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum, with mild heterogeneous enhancement after IV contrast and bone remodeling. There was no extension into the paranasal sinuses or apparent bone invasion.. Confirmed diagnosis: Nasal Septal Schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: Nasal Septal Schwannoma.

Interpretation of findings:

Sudden onset after significant head trauma or toxin exposure strongly

implicates that event as the cause.

A history of chronic rhinosinusitis is suggestive, particularly when significant congestion, polyps, or both

are visible on examination. However, because these findings are common in the population, the physician

should be wary of missing another disorder. Progressive confusion and recent memory loss in an elderly

patient suggest Alzheimer's disease as a cause. Waxing and waning neurologic symptoms affecting

multiple areas suggest a neurodegenerative disease such as multiple sclerosis. Slowly progressive

anosmia in an elderly patient with no other symptoms or findings suggests normal aging as the cause.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 31-year-old male of Eastern European origin presented with a 3-month history of unilateral nasal obstruction, swelling, and sporadic, short-lasting episodes of epistaxis. He reported swelling of the right lateral nasal wall. Examination revealed a large, right-sided nasal polypoidal mass occluding most of the right nasal airway. The mucosa appeared smooth and healthy, but the nasal septum was significantly deviated to the left. Endoscopic examination of the pharynx, larynx, and contralateral side of the nose was normal. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy, and the rest of the ear, nose, and throat, as well as physical examinations, were normal. Non-contrast CT of the sinonasal region showed a soft tissue lesion arising from the right side of the nasal septum. MRI imaging of the lesion indicated a general increased T2 signal with heterogeneous nodular T2 heterogeneity. The unenhanced axial T1-weighted sequence revealed a small focus of T1 shortening, consistent with low volume focal cystic degeneration within the tumor.. Confirmed diagnosis: nasal septal schwannoma. Differential diagnosis includes: nasal septal schwannoma.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 70-year-old male reported experiencing mild pain, watering, and discharges from his left eye, along with restricted eye movement for six months. His medical history was unremarkable except for participation in a community bath. Upon examination, his vision was measured at 20/40, and he had a senile cataract. The globe was intact, with mild ptosis and restricted eye movement in all lateral directions. Intra-ocular pressure (IOP) was normal, and there was regurgitation of pressure over the lacrimal sac. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the left orbit in axial and coronal planes depicted a predominantly intraconal soft tissue density mass lesion measuring 2.5 (AP) × 1.5 (ML) × 1.5 (CC) cm3 involving the medial rectus and posterior aspect of the superior rectus muscle. MRI revealed a well-defined T2 hypointense lesion in the left orbit involving the medial rectus and extending to the postero-medial aspect of the superior rectus, abutting the lateral part of the left optic nerve sheath. It was heterogeneously enhanced with contrast.. Confirmed diagnosis: Intra-Orbital Wooden Foreign Body. Differential diagnosis includes: Intra-Orbital Wooden Foreign Body.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 40-year-old male presented with a 10-month history of watery nasal discharge. He also reported a history of headaches and nasal obstruction, previously attributed to hypertrophied turbinate, for which surgery was recommended but declined. Over the past 2 years, the patient experienced a gradual onset of anosmia, initially without watery discharge but associated with nasal obstruction. The watery nasal discharge increased when bending forward or coughing and trickled into the nasopharynx without any detectable taste. This discharge was also associated with headaches. The patient has no history of nasal trauma, surgery, or signs of meningitis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele. Differential diagnosis includes: Spontaneous Lateral Intrasphenoidal Encephalocele.

Diagnosis is suspected clinically. Other disorders to consider include trauma, insect or animal bites

without cellulitis, retained foreign bodies, allergic reactions, tumors, and inflammatory orbital

pseudotumor.

Eyelid swelling may require the use of lid retractors for evaluation of the globe, and initial signs of

complicated infection may be subtle. An ophthalmologist should be consulted when orbital cellulitis is

suspected.

Preseptal cellulitis and orbital cellulitis are often distinguishable clinically. Preseptal cellulitis is likely if eye

findings are normal except for eyelid swelling. The presence of a local nidus of infection on the skin

makes preseptal cellulitis even more likely.

If findings are equivocal, if the examination is difficult (as in young children), or if nasal discharge is

present (suggesting sinusitis), CT or MRI should be done to confirm orbital cellulitis, to exclude tumor and

pseudotumor, and to diagnose sinusitis if present. MRI is better than CT if cavernous sinus thrombosis is

being considered.

The direction of proptosis may be a clue to the site of infection; eg, extension from the frontal sinus

pushes the globe down and out, and extension from the ethmoid sinus pushes the globe laterally and out.

Blood cultures are often done (ideally before beginning antibiotics) in patients with orbital cellulitis but are

positive in less than one third. Lumbar puncture is done if meningitis is suspected. Cultures of the

paranasal sinus fluid are done if sinusitis is the suspected source. Other laboratory tests are not

Vital signs are reviewed, particularly for presence of fever.

The nose is examined for discharge and foreign body.

The mouth is examined for signs of gum disease, dental infection, and cancer. Signs of apparent dryness

are noted (eg, whether the mucosa is dry, sticky, or moist; whether saliva is foamy, stringy, or normal in

appearance).

The pharynx is examined for signs of infection and cancer.

Sniff test:

A sniff test of exhaled air is conducted. In general, oral causes result in a putrefying, pungent

smell, whereas systemic conditions result in a more subtle, abnormal odor. Ideally, for 48 h before the

examination, the patient avoids eating garlic or onions, and for 2 h before, the patient abstains from

eating,

chewing, drinking, gargling, rinsing, or smoking. During the test, the patient exhales 10 cm away

from the examiner's nose, first through the mouth and then with the mouth closed. A worse odor through

the mouth suggests an oral etiology. A worse odor through the nose suggests a nasal or sinus etiology.

Similar odor through both nose and mouth suggests a systemic or pulmonary cause. If site of origin is

unclear, the posterior tongue is scraped with a plastic spoon. After 5 sec, the spoon is sniffed 5 cm from

the examiner's nose.

excerpts.text: Presentation: A 9-year-old boy presented with low-grade fever, chest pain, breathlessness, and thick yellow nasal discharge. He had a history of treatment for allergic sinusitis and bronchial asthma since the age of 3. At 4 years old, he was treated with anti-tuberculosis therapy due to small opacities in the lung observed radiologically, despite being sputum negative. He also reported expectoration with brown-colored sputum. Over the years, he received multiple treatments including antibiotics, antihistamines, corticosteroids (both nasal and inhaled), and bronchodilators, but his symptoms persisted. Upon examination, his temperature was 96°F (axillary), pulse rate was 84/min, respiratory rate was 16/min, and blood pressure was 110/60 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi. Peripheral blood examination showed eosinophilia at 8%, hemoglobin at 11 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate at 12 mm/hour, and white blood cell count at 8,400 cells/cm³.. Confirmed diagnosis: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis with Aspergillus Sinusitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis with Aspergillus Sinusitis.

Additionally, he experienced abdominal pain and melena for the past month. The patient also presented with rashes on his face, trunk, limbs, and feet, as well as oral ulcers, perianal ulcers, and sinusitis. Leucocytes count of 8.5 × 109/L, hemoglobin level of 79 g/L, urine protein (+), microhematuria (+), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h, c-ANCA with a titre of 1 in 100, and PR3-ANCA of > 200 RU/ml. CT revealed left frontal and ethmoid sinusitis, and bilateral maxillary sinusitis. Colonic biopsies revealed inflammatory granulation tissues. The membrane biopsy revealed degenerative colonic mucosal tissues, while the colonic biopsy revealed inflammatory granulation tissues without normal colon glands.. Confirmed diagnosis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis. Differential diagnosis includes: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.

Interpretation of findings:

The distinction between acute and chronic stridor is important. Other clinical

findings are also often helpful (see

).

Acute manifestations are more likely to reflect an immediately life-threatening disorder. With these

disorders, fever indicates infection. Fever plus barking cough suggests croup or, very rarely, tracheitis.

Patients with croup typically have more prominent URI symptoms and less of a toxic appearance. Fever

without cough, particularly if accompanied by toxic appearance, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, or

respiratory distress, suggests epiglottitis and, in young children, the less common retropharyngeal

abscess. Drooling and the tripod position are suggestive of epiglottitis, whereas retropharyngeal abscess

may manifest with neck stiffness and inability to extend the neck.

Patients without fever or URI symptoms may have an acute allergic reaction or aspirated foreign body.

Acute allergic reaction severe enough to cause stridor usually has other manifestations of airway edema

(eg, oral or facial edema, wheezing) or anaphylaxis (itching, urticaria). Foreign body obstruction of the

upper airway that causes stridor is always acute but may be occult in toddlers (older children and adults

can communicate the event unless there is near-complete airway obstruction, which will manifest as such,

not as stridor). Cough is often present with foreign body but rare with allergic reaction.

Chronic stridor that begins early in childhood and without a clear inciting factor suggests a congenital

In

bubonic plague,

the most common form, the incubation period is usually 2 to 5 days but varies from a

few hours to 12 days. Onset of fever of 39.5 to 41° C is abrupt, often with chills. The pulse may be rapid

and thready; hypotension may occur. Enlarged lymph nodes (buboes) appear with or shortly after the

fever. The femoral or inguinal lymph nodes are most commonly involved, followed by axillary, cervical, or

multiple nodes. Typically, the nodes are extremely tender and firm, surrounded by considerable edema.

They may suppurate in the 2nd wk. The overlying skin is smooth and reddened but often not warm. A

primary cutaneous lesion, varying from a small vesicle with slight local lymphangitis to an eschar,

occasionally appears at the bite. The patient may be restless, delirious, confused, and uncoordinated.

The liver and spleen may be enlarged. Bubonic plague may be complicated by pneumonic plague.

Primary pneumonic plague

has a 2- to 3-day incubation period, followed by abrupt onset of high fever,

chills, tachycardia, chest pain, and headache, often severe. Cough, not prominent initially, develops within

24 h. Sputum is mucoid at first, rapidly develops blood specks, and then becomes uniformly pink or bright

red (resembling raspberry syrup) and foamy. Tachypnea and dyspnea are present, but pleuritic chest pain

is not. Signs of consolidation are rare, and rales may be absent.
